#5119. Bitcoin ETFs shed $4 billion — How did one fund hide the cracks before leading the exit?

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

U.S Spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $4.14 billion over three weeks, with BlackRock’s IBIT accounting for roughly 84% of the withdrawals. However, the same fund had been concealing weakness elsewhere just weeks ago. The story behind the numbers is considerably more complicated than the headline.

In the week leading up to October 19, U.S Spot Bitcoin ETFs appeared to be doing rather well. The funds collectively attracted $301.2 million in net inflows. That’s quite a reassuring development for a market that had become accustomed to treating ETF demand as a barometer of Bitcoin’s institutional appeal.

There was one small complication, though. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) had brought in $565.7 million on its own. Every other fund combined lost $264.5 million. So, how healthy was that $301.2 million gain if it depended entirely on one fund?

Three weeks later, the answer became harder to ignore.

Between November 2 and 20, Bitcoin ETFs suffered a staggering $4.14 billion in net withdrawals, according to Farside Investors. By the way, IBIT ALONE accounted for approximately $3.49 billion, or 84% of the exodus.

And the selling gathered pace as the week wore on. Nearly $1.79 billion left in the final week, around 1.7 times the previous week’s withdrawals. From November 17 through November 20, each trading session ended with a larger outflow than the previous one.

October’s biggest source of support had become November’s biggest source of pressure. The reversal was striking enough. In fact, what was happening beneath it was more revealing!

BlackRock’s influence on the industry’s performance was hardly a one-week curiosity.

The pattern continued into October 26–30. IBIT attracted another $176.9 million while competing funds collectively lost $379.3 million. Even though the industry finished that week in the red, BlackRock’s inflows effectively absorbed nearly half the damage.

Spot BTC ETFs recorded roughly $643 million in withdrawals in a single session, with IBIT contributing approximately $234 million. The fund that had been cushioning the industry’s losses was now participating in them.

November made that reversal unmistakable.

IBIT accounted for approximately 94% of the industry’s net outflows during the first week, 85% during the second, and 76% during the third. Curiously, its share declined even as the third week brought the industry’s biggest outflow yet.

That was the more consequential development. Other funds, including Fidelity’s FBTC and products from Grayscale and ARK, were contributing increasingly to the selling. What had initially been concentrated overwhelmingly in BlackRock’s product was beginning to spread.

A market once held up by its largest fund was now being dragged down by it, with competitors increasingly joining the retreat.

Now, IBIT was already by far the industry’s biggest fund. Perhaps its dominance in the withdrawals was simply a consequence of its size. Hence why that possibility deserved a closer look. However, a closer look at this position revealed another complication.

A fund holding most of the industry’s assets will naturally account for a significant share of its movements. A billion dollars leaving a $60 billion product is hardly equivalent to the same amount leaving one worth $5 billion.

By October 30, IBIT held approximately $62.7 billion in Bitcoin, according to iShares holdings data. Looking at it broadly, the Bitcoin ETF market held roughly $98.14 billion, based on SoSoValue.

BlackRock therefore controlled about two-thirds of the industry’s assets entering November. And yet, it accounted for 84% of the subsequent three-week net withdrawals.

The disparity only becomes sharper when adjusted for size.

IBIT’s $3.49 billion outflow was equivalent to approximately 5.6% of its starting holdings value. For all the other funds combined, the equivalent was just 1.8%.

In relative terms, BlackRock’s fund experienced roughly three times the withdrawal pressure of its competitors. Its scale explained part of its dominance, but hardly all of it.

The underlying Bitcoin inventory tells a similar story. IBIT held approximately 811,817 BTC on October 30. By November 20, that had fallen to roughly 760,926 BTC, a reduction of nearly 50,900 BTC or 6.3%.

Bitcoin’s declining price could reduce the dollar value of those holdings, but it could not account for the disappearance of the coins themselves. IBIT’s inventory had genuinely contracted.

The departures were measurable. The identities of those departing were another matter.

A $4 billion ETF outflow makes it tempting to declare that institutional investors are abandoning Bitcoin. Yet the available data cannot distinguish an asset manager reducing exposure from an individual investor selling shares, or a market participant unwinding a hedged position.

Nor does it establish whether the capital left Bitcoin altogether or found another route back into the market. That uncertainty matters because the industry has grown comfortable treating ETF inflows as evidence of institutional conviction. Applying the opposite interpretation to withdrawals may be tempting, but it is no more conclusive.

What November demonstrated was a substantial withdrawal of capital from these investment products, led disproportionately by BlackRock’s IBIT.

Whether it represented a broader loss of faith in Bitcoin was a considerably larger question though.

And while investors were heading for the exits, there seemed to be little indication that the fund itself had stopped functioning as intended.

There is an understandable tendency to interpret large ETF outflows as a sign that the investment product itself has somehow failed. However, IBIT’s trading data tells us a more measured story.

According to iShares, IBIT closed at $33.02 on November 20 against a net asset value of $33.05, a discount of about 0.10%. Its 30-day median bid-ask spread was 0.02%. In other words, the fund traded almost exactly at the value of the Bitcoin it holds, even as markets were falling.

Trading was heavy. About 109.2 million IBIT shares changed hands on November 20, more than twice the fund’s 30-day average of about 50.1 million.

That is not the same as money leaving the fund though because trading volume is not net flow. A 30-day median spread also doesn’t show that trading stayed cheap at every volatile moment.

Still, nothing here suggests investors were fleeing a broken product. They were trading a working fund whose underlying asset had dropped sharply. IBIT’s NAV fell $2.08 (5.92%) on November 20 to $33.05, and its NAV total return for 2026 stood at −29.06% as of November 19.

Wall Street made Bitcoin easier to buy. That was never the same promise as making it safer to hold. That distinction matters for the question that comes next — how much of the fall in ETF assets was money leaving, and how much was the price?

According to SoSoValue, combined Spot Bitcoin ETF assets reached approximately $110.8 billion on October 5. By November 20, they had fallen to roughly $71.3 billion.

A decline approaching $39.5 billion sounds extraordinary beside three weeks of approximately $4.14 billion in net withdrawals.

However, assets under management represent the market value of what these funds hold. That value changes both when investors create or redeem shares and when Bitcoin itself rises or falls.

Using Coinbase Bitcoin prices recorded by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, Bitcoin fell from approximately $85,821 on October 5 to $58,831 on November 20 — A fall of 31.4%.

Over the same period, reported ETF assets fell by approximately 36%.

Such a comparison strongly suggests that Bitcoin’s price decline accounted for much of the reduction in ETF asset values. It is not a precise decomposition — flows occurred throughout the period, holdings changed, and the dates and valuation methodologies must be matched before assigning an exact proportion to each driver.

Still, the broad conclusion is difficult to miss.

Tens of billions of dollars can disappear from reported fund asset values without an equivalent sum being withdrawn by investors. A falling portfolio value and a redeemed investment are two different financial events. Treating them interchangeably gives a dramatic headline considerably more authority than it deserves.

Bitcoin’s ETF market was not the only place seeing withdrawals either.

From November 9 to 13, U.S Spot Ether ETFs lost about $398.9 million, according to Farside. BlackRock’s iShares Ethereum Trust (ETHA) accounted for about $311.1 million of that, or 78%. The following week, Ether funds lost about $306 million, with ETHA responsible for about $230 million or 75%.

That’s the same pattern we saw in Bitcoin — one BlackRock fund carrying most of the headline outflow.

Stablecoins told a slower story. According to DefiLlama, their combined market capitalisation was about $295.3 billion on October 30. It fell to $290.2 billion by November 6, $285.6 billion by November 13, and $281.3 billion by November 20. That is a contraction of about $14 billion, or 4.8%, in three weeks.

Unlike the ETF flows, which peaked in the final week, stablecoins shrank at a fairly steady pace — about $5.1 billion, $4.6 billion, then $4.3 billion a week.

Stablecoins are the dollar-pegged tokens traders use for settlement, trading balances, and collateral. So, a falling supply suggests liquidity may be tightening beyond the regulated ETF market. The two trends overlapped, but they moved at different speeds.

Bitcoin’s own trading schedule adds a complication too.

FRED’s Coinbase series showed Bitcoin falling from about $68,178 on November 13 to $62,891 on November 14, a drop of 7.8%, after that week’s ETF sessions ended.

However, after the much heavier withdrawal week ending November 20, Bitcoin went the other way. It fell from about $58,831 on November 20 to $60,992 on November 22 — A gain of 3.7%.

Two weekends prove nothing on their own, and FRED’s prices are taken at 5 p.m Pacific, not at the ETF close. But they do show that a record ETF outflow and a falling price don’t move in lockstep.

There is no need to minimise the withdrawals. About $4.14 billion in three weeks is a major reversal, particularly when the final week was the worst of the three.

Nor should IBIT’s concentration be brushed off as a consequence of its size. Its 84% share of the net outflows exceeded its roughly two-thirds share of starting industry assets.

However, context changes the interpretation.

SoSoValue’s November 20 figures still showed about $52.8 billion in cumulative net inflows since January 2024. That is down roughly $4 billion from where November began, but nearly three years of accumulated inflows were not erased by three difficult weeks.

October offers a useful warning about reading any headline in isolation. The same fund that masked withdrawals elsewhere in two October weeks went on to account for most of November’s exits. The industry totals recorded both developments accurately, yet told very different stories depending on whether you looked at the funds behind them.

The ETF structure broadened access to Bitcoin. It also gave investors a familiar, liquid way to reduce exposure. Neither is a guarantee about Bitcoin’s price.

Perhaps institutions were cutting risk. Or, retail investors may have been heading for the exits. Others could simply have been unwinding complex positions that had little to do with long-term conviction in Bitcoin. All three are plausible explanations.

What they do establish is narrower but more useful — the withdrawals were substantial, heavily concentrated in one product, and increasingly shared across competing funds as November went on.

So, the next time a billion-dollar ETF outflow makes the headlines, the interesting questions begin after the headline. Which funds accounted for it? How large were the withdrawals relative to their assets? Is the number money leaving a product, or is the market value of its holdings falling?

And one more, which no flow table can answer — Who was actually selling?

#5117. Zcash (ZEC) Holders Get Key Update as Gemini Adds Shielded Deposit Support

Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. Zcash holders just got a new update as the major crypto exchange Gemini has announced support for Shielded Zcash deposits.

Scott Merkel, 'Wolf of All Streets,' shared this update in an X post, highlighting the milestone as the first of its kind for any major exchange. According to Merkel, Gemini now lets customers deposit Zcash (ZEC) to shielded addresses, saying it is the first major exchange with both shielded deposits and withdrawals.

GEMINI NOW LETS CUSTOMERS DEPOSIT ZCASH $ZEC TO SHIELDED ADDRESSES, SAYING IT IS THE FIRST MAJOR EXCHANGE WITH BOTH SHIELDED DEPOSITS AND WITHDRAWALS https://t.co/d9pIFJ6uJM

Gemini co-founder Tyler Winklevoss shared the milestone in a recent X post, adding that the recent move builds on the launch of shielded Zcash withdrawals on Gemini this summer.

In July 2026, shortly after the Ironwood upgrade was activated, Gemini launched support for shielded Zcash withdrawals to the new Ironwood pool, allowing users to send Zcash from Gemini to their Ironwood deposit address. Ironwood (NU6.3) went live on July 28, 2026, at block height 3,428,143, bringing a new shielded pool for Zcash.

With the recent launch of support for Shielded Zcash deposits, Gemini users can make Shielded Zcash deposits and withdrawals to and from Ironwood, with Winklevoss remarking that the private movement of money was now complete.

Zcash's total shielded supply now sits at around 4.93 million ZEC (around 28.94% of total ZEC supply) as of November 25, 2026.

November has brought in key updates for the Zcash network. Zcash's NU7 upgrade went live earlier in November 2026, slashing ZEC's target block time to 25 seconds from 75 seconds. The new 25-second block target lets miners add a batch of transactions to the chain three times as often.

None of this prints extra ZEC. Each block pays a third as much and halvings come every 5,040,000 blocks instead of 1,680,000, so the issuance schedule holds at roughly four years per halving.

Days after the NU7 upgrade, the Zcash Foundation followed up with the release of Zebra 7.1.0, which fixed ten security advisories, most of which closed off ways in which another node on the network (a peer) could stop a Zebra node from catching up with the chain or make it run out of memory. It also added sync and memory diagnostics, automatic peer recovery, and clearer errors.

#5116. Could Bitwise’s $667M XRP ETF inflows come to the rescue as bear trap takes shape?

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Bitwise has released its annual XRP ETF report.

According to the report, the ETF has seen net cash flows of $667 million since it began trading on the NYSE in November 2025. Meanwhile, assets under management were in excess of $376 million while total trading crossed $3.5 billion, averaging around $14 million a day.

In essence, despite XRP’s lackluster performance, interest in the ETF continues to receive institutional investment, implying a high level of investor demand.

In a post on X, Bitwise highlighted XRP’s decade-long presence in the crypto market. It also noted how the asset has remained relevant through multiple market cycles and continues to shape the industry’s future.

XRP has been part of crypto’s story for more than a decade, through every cycle, and it’s still helping shape what comes next. We’re grateful to everyone who’s been part of the journey so far. Here’s to year two!

The timing is particularly interesting here.

Bitwise’s report comes as XRP’s technical and on-chain metrics continue to deteriorate. Meanwhile, prediction markets are also increasingly pricing in a year-end target below $0.80. Against this backdrop, the key question is whether Bitwise’s report can strengthen institutional interest and turn the current bearish setup into a bear trap.

The impact of Bitwise’s one-year XRP ETF performance could already be triggering FOMO.

Notably, another Wall Street firm has disclosed exposure to an XRP ETF. Atlanta-based Arkadios Wealth Advisors, which looks after $8.79 billion in client assets, stated this in its most recent SEC document.

Furthermore, there is some institutional interest in Turkiye too. One of the nation’s biggest private banks, Yapi Kredi, is leveraging Ripple Custody to provide digital asset security solutions.

The key takeaway? XRP’s derivatives continue to be significantly net short, with the long/short ratio showing a pronounced sell-side sentiment. At the time of writing, XRP seemed set to close its 10th consecutive weekly down candle, with broader market FUD and prediction markets pricing in a year-end target below $0.80 to reinforce the cautious outlook.

Interestingly, however, the XRP/BTC ratio has risen by almost 5% following three successive weeks of upside.

In essence, broader market weakness could create room for more capital to flow into XRP.

This makes it an important setup to watch over the coming months. The logic is simple —  Entering Q4, market participants are already factoring in further downside potential. In this context, Bitwise’s recent report, growing ETF exposure, and Ripple’s expansion in Turkiye could encourage further capital rotation into XRP.

If this trend continues, XRP’s ongoing consolidation around $0.90 could turn out to be an accumulation phase before a potential bear trap.

Bitwise’s XRP ETF has attracted $667 million in net inflows, while growing institutional exposure and Ripple’s expansion in Turkiye point to sustained demand.

Despite bearish derivatives and weakening market sentiment, rising XRP/BTC strength could signal a potential accumulation phase.

#5115. XRP Pattern Recalls Structure Behind 190% Rally

Home » Ripple (XRP) » XRP Pattern Recalls Structure Behind 190% Rally

A new research paper identifies striking similarities between the current market and November 2022.

XRP’s price setup has printed higher highs in crypto charts on a monthly basis. With traders trying to locate the local price bottom, speculative positions are winding down on Perpetual markets. These two conflicting signals present a setup that has been witnessed once in 2022.

Recently, Turkish analyst Celal Kucuker dived into the monthly chart from Bitstamp, which shows XRP near $1 with an ascending green trend-line and price projections indicating potential moves to $3.19 and $5.94. The seasoned analyst framed $5 as achievable in the longer-term.

$XRP has one of the best-looking charts in the market.XRP has maintained a rising trendline since 2014 ts long-term chart structure is remarkable. $5 and beyond is certainly not a fantasy. pic.twitter.com/Wuvq7P3D0E

The X post attracted 522 likes and 31k views with mixed replies questioning near-term catalysts. He called XRP’ monthly setup “one of the best-looking charts”, adding that XRP has maintained a rising trendline formation since 2014, positioning $3.19 as the initial target in the next bull run.

The sentiment is bitter & the market mood resembles that of November 2022, latest research from Bitrue’s Research Institute states. The analysts at Bitrue analyzed a multi-cycle market data bundle from 2022 to 2026, showcasing similar levels of ‘extreme fear’ around 20.

Back in 2022, FTX fiasco has ambushed the global crypto markets with an uncalled for liquidation event erasing billions of dollars a day for consecutive weeks. The downswings in market value are also similar.

XRP’s cycle drawdown stands at 77% now in comparison to 81% then. Crypto chart analyst Cleo Schmidt marked a series of ‘bull-traps’ prior to XRP spiking by 1,000% and 800% during the bull runs back in 2021 & 2024.

$XRP keeps repeating the same pattern.A false bottom.A bull trap.A period of range-bound consolidation.And only then, the real bottom.Every previous rally has begun after this sequence, not during it.The chart is currently in that intermediate phase.The "launchpad" isn't… pic.twitter.com/OehoKC8hSX

Schmidt’s chart examines XRP’s weekly price from 2017 through 2026, highlighting nearly-identical patterns across several market cycles.

Two months from the FTX-infused crypto beatdown, XRP’s holders roughly gained 190% from the recorded XRP price on November 21, 2022. It took them 8 months to gain 115%, but the OG altcoin backtracked to 60% of yearly gains one year after the FTX collapse.

Surely, the 190% pattern could play out quicker with proper demand. With Ripple scoring new regulatory winnings, the compliance leadership doesn’t necessarily translate into XRP’s price appreciation. A part of that is attributed to the rise of stablecoins, along with Ripple’s RLUSD.

On the other hand, Bitrue Research Institute offers some encouragement in their Futures market data findings. Since 2017, XRP’s price has finished below $1 six times on a weekly basis, but restored that level each time.

The historical XRP price comparison heavily relies on holding the $0.859 support. Shaking below would basically invalidate the bullish thesis based on XRP’s price history.

Aside from technicals, institutions may pick it up: heading into 2027, ETFs will play a pivotal role in XRP’s bounce back attempt.

#5114. Tesla Cybercab’s autonomy agreement is insane: $299/mo or it doesn’t move

Tesla has posted the agreement that comes with its $29,990 Cybercab, and it’s even worse than the order page suggested. The two-seater can’t move without a $299 monthly “Autonomy Subscription” that Tesla can reprice with a month’s notice, suspend for a week, or cut off entirely.

And Tesla wants consumers to sign it while still refusing to give unsupervised self-driving to the Model Y owners it has been selling “Full Self-Driving” to for nearly a decade.

The “Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement” (version 20261112) went up on Tesla’s configurator late Friday, hours after the company started inviting select customers to order the Cybercab for personal use at $29,990 plus a mandatory $299 per month.

The key line is short: “Your Cybercab will not operate without an active Autonomy Subscription.” There’s no steering wheel and no pedals, so that isn’t a figure of speech. Stop paying and you have a $30,000 object in your garage.

That personal-use clause kills the whole pitch. For years, Musk told people they’d buy a Tesla, add it to the fleet, and make money while they sleep. The first Tesla sold to consumers for unsupervised operation is contractually barred from doing exactly that.

Then there’s the geofence. Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas are already smaller in practice than advertised: when we tested them, real coverage was between 59% and 78% of the advertised maps, and parts of the Houston map have been called “fake” by the person tracking it. Now Tesla reserves the right to shrink that area after you’ve paid for the car.

Mark Valorian, who went through the terms on X, summed it up as “an endless variable-rate lease with a ridiculous down payment.” That’s about right.

Over five years, the car plus 59 paid months of subscription comes to $47,631 before insurance, registration, charging, and taxes, all of which are on the owner.

This is the part that should make every Tesla owner angry.

Tesla has spent the last year telling everyone that its Model Y is just as much a robotaxi as the Cybercab. Ahead of the Robotaxi launch in Austin, Musk said the cars were “the Model Ys we make currently, there’s no change to it.” On Tesla’s Q3 2026 earnings call last month, AI chief Ashok Elluswamy said Cybercabs and Model Y robotaxis already run the same software, and that customer cars might join the network around Q2 2027. The Cybercab launches on the same AI4 computer found in the current Model Y.

So the hardware is the same, the software is the same, and unsupervised Model Ys are already operating in the exact geofences where Cybercab owners will be allowed to ride.

Yet the people who paid for it get nothing. Tesla started selling “Full Self-Driving Capability” in 2016 on the promise that every car it built had the hardware for it. Owners paid up to $15,000 for the package. In February, Tesla stopped selling it outright and moved to a $99 per month subscription, which still requires you to supervise the car at all times.

Tesla’s answer to all those owners is a new car. One with two seats, no controls, a geofence it can move whenever it wants, and a subscription that costs three times as much as FSD.

I’ll say it plainly: this car is for suckers who want to give their money to Elon Musk.

You don’t own a Cybercab in any meaningful sense. You pay $30,000 for the right to keep paying Tesla $299 a month, at a price Tesla can raise, in an area Tesla can shrink, under rules Tesla enforces, with a camera pointed at you the whole time.

There are three possible reasons Tesla isn't allowing model Y owners to use FSD in the allowed zones:

1: the robotaxis are in fact different from the model Ys being sold

2: Tesla doesn't have enough "remote operators" to cover all of those supposedly self-driving cars if users join the network

3: Tesla isn't willing to accept liability when FSD kills someone.

And the Model Y part is what gives the game away. If Tesla truly believed its unsupervised system was ready for customers, the obvious move would be to turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin who already paid for it. It’s the same computer and the same software in the same geofence. But that would mean honoring a promise made in 2016, on cars already sold, with no new revenue attached.

A new vehicle wipes that slate clean. No legacy FSD buyers, no HW3 baggage, just a fresh customer locked into a $299 monthly fee from day one. What Tesla built is a subscription with a $30,000 entry fee attached to it.

So what happens the first time Tesla emails Cybercab owners a month’s notice that the price is going to $399?

#5110. Ukraine Legalizes Crypto After One-Day Delay

Home » Regulations » Ukraine Legalizes Crypto After One-Day Delay

Crypto-embracing Bill No. 10225-d gets the highest-priority treatment following a slight procedural delay.

Ukraine’s parliament has approved a bill to bring cryptocurrency trading, custody and taxation under a formal legal framework.

The measure, Bill No. 10225-d, passed after lawmakers postponed consideration a day earlier, a pause that had raised questions about its immediate path despite renewed support from the parliamentary finance committee for the revised text.

The Ukraine crypto bill is designed to legalize and regulate the domestic virtual-asset market rather than leave it in a largely undefined legal space.

Its scope includes tax treatment for crypto activity as well as rules for trading platforms and custodial services.

That approach would place businesses handling customer assets under a clearer licensing and compliance structure.

BREAKING: Ukraine officially passes law to LEGALIZE crypto, effective July 1, 2027. pic.twitter.com/6KxnNa7N2b

The framework comes into practice on July 1, 2027. It offers more certainty over how digital-asset transactions are treated by authorities, though implementation details will matter as much as the legislation itself.

Ukraine has maintained an active crypto sector despite the strains of war, with digital assets playing a visible role in fundraising and cross-border transfers.

Formalizing the market has therefore carried significance beyond ordinary financial regulation: it could help define how crypto businesses operate in an economy still managing exceptional pressures with the fifth year of war with Russia coming along.

The Ukraine crypto bill’s journey shows how quickly crypto policy can shift even when lawmakers broadly support regulation.

BREAKING: Zelensky President of Ukraine officially legalizes Bitcoin & crypto after parliament passes the bill with 271 vote pic.twitter.com/qt9C7jcNVK

The November 24, 2026 postponement followed committee backing for a revised version, while the subsequent passage points to a resolution of at least some of those immediate obstacles.

Questions remain over the final tax mechanics, the timing of licensing requirements and which agencies will oversee different parts of the sector. Market participants will also watch for secondary rules that determine the practical burden on exchanges, brokers and wallet providers.

Ukraine’s crypto move matters because it adds another sizable European market pursuing rules for digital assets rather than relying on prohibition or legal ambiguity.

The Ukraine crypto legislation may give local firms a route toward greater legitimacy, but the ultimate test will be whether the resulting framework is workable enough to retain innovation while improving crypto oversight.

#5107. French Senate Rejects Disclosure Rule for Crypto

French senators on Nov. 24 rejected a proposal that would have required taxpayers to disclose self-hosted cryptocurrency holdings exceeding €100,000.

They would have had to report those assets as of Dec. 31.

This would have been the case even if they had held the same coins since January without making any sales.

Two matching amendments to the French 2027 budget were rejected by the Senate during the first reading of the draft.

Senators Pascal Savoldelli and Anne-Sophie Romagny reintroduced the proposal after it briefly passed in the National Assembly earlier in the month.

French taxpayers must disclose their crypto assets held on foreign crypto platforms.

These amendments would have expanded disclosure requirements to wallets that owners directly control. This pertains to a wallet that is not managed by an exchange or another custodian.

The French National Assembly approved the €100,000 disclosure threshold in a 150-44 vote on Nov. 3. There were also eight abstentions.

The next day, the National Assembly voted down the entire revenue portion of the budget.

This vote brought down the wallet disclosure provision along with the rest of the budget.

However, the subsequent effort to revive the provision in the Senate was defeated.

It should be noted that the 2027 budget is still being considered at the time of writing.

The Senate also rejected two other crypto-related measures debated as part of the budget.

One was a provision to tax gains realized when holders exchange cryptocurrencies for certain stablecoins.

The second was a proposal to expand France's exit tax to include unrealized gains on cryptocurrencies held by taxpayers who move their tax residence outside the country.

#5106. Ethereum maps post-AI, post-quantum cryptographic overhaul with Keccak-256 — Details

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Ethereum Foundation is in the news today after it announced that it has recommended Keccak-256 as the hash function for Ethereum’s hash-based cryptography.

The ongoing bear market price action is only a bump in the road. In the long term, however, the network has to be prepared to contend with threats posed by both quantum computing and progressing artificial intelligence capabilities.

On Tuesday, 24th November, the Foundation revealed its recommendation and the reasons behind it.

It considered five candidates: the ZK-friendly hashes, Poseidon and Poseidon2, the fast hashes BLAKE3 and BLAKE2, and the two hashes Ethereum already uses- SHA-256 and Keccak-256.

Keccak-256 has “arguably the most extensive cryptanalysis out of all unbroken traditional hashes,” the blog post read. An additional benefit is that this hash function has so far remained unaffected by AI-assisted cryptanalysis

Zero-knowledge proof technology improvements have removed the performance advantages offered by Poseidon. Security was the primary concern.

Though natively fast, the best collision attack reached 38 out of 64 rounds for SHA-256. Only 5 out of 24 rounds were reached for Keccak-256.

The Foundation also recommended against using SHA3-256 alongside Keccak-256 since both use the same underlying permutation and have similar security characteristics.

According to Ethereum Foundation Researcher Kev Wedderburn, they have been planning ways to counter quantum computing’s threat. In fact, AI has emerged as a more urgent risk recently.

Models are already finding bugs in production software faster than people can review them, the researcher wrote.

The planned upgrade will overhaul how validators sign messages, users authorize transactions, and how Ethereum verifies data posted by rollups.

It is harder than the 2022 Merge, and there is less time, Wedderburn acknowledged. Working faster can ship more bugs, so the Foundation has doubled the protocol security team to ensure formal verification. This will also allow the security work to progress at the pace of protocol development.

#5105. Switzerland’s First Spot Bitcoin ETF BBIT Begins Trading on SIX

Home » Bitcoin (BTC) » Switzerland’s First Spot Bitcoin ETF BBIT Begins Trading on SIX

BIT Asset Management’s regulated fund brings direct spot Bitcoin access to Swiss retail accounts.

BIT Asset Management’s Bitcoin Fund ETF (BBIT), Switzerland’s first spot Bitcoin exchange-traded fund, began trading on the SIX Swiss Exchange on November 26, 2026. Structured as a regulated Swiss collective investment fund, the product gives retail investors direct Bitcoin exposure through standard Swiss bank or brokerage accounts without self-custody.

The passive fund tracks the SIX Bitcoin Reference Rate and holds physical Bitcoin offline in cold storage at regulated Swiss custodian AMINA Bank AG, ring-fenced from the manager’s and custodian’s own assets.

BIT Asset Management describes BBIT as Europe’s currently active spot Bitcoin ETF, though public offering is approved only in Switzerland.

BBIT is listed on SIX Swiss Exchange and trades in both U.S. dollars and Swiss francs, with a target annual management fee of 0.19%. The fund launched with an initial issue price of $10 per unit and an allocation of 350 BTC, valued at more than $20 million at launch.

Switzerland’s Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA) approved BBIT’s fund contract on October 20, 2026, following an 18-month review.

FINMA granted an exemption from standard investment diversification requirements, allowing the fund to invest exclusively in Bitcoin based on the cryptocurrency’s established trading history and liquidity.

However, the fund is classified as an alternative investment fund with specific risks, reflecting Bitcoin’s volatility and potential for substantial capital losses.

Unlike most European crypto exchange-traded products, which are structured as debt instruments and expose investors to issuer credit risk, BBIT operates under Swiss collective investment scheme legislation. This means investors hold fund units backed by ring-fenced assets, legally separated from the fund management company’s own assets.

Pernet von Ballmoos AG (PvB) acts as the fund management company and issuer, while BIT Asset Management serves as the sponsor and investment manager. Flow Traders has been appointed as the market maker, supporting secondary-market liquidity.

The fund also provides daily disclosure of its Bitcoin holdings and supports in-kind subscriptions for eligible institutional participants.

While BBIT is Switzerland’s first retail spot Bitcoin ETF, a physically backed Bitcoin product—the Jacobi FT Wilshire Bitcoin ETF—previously debuted on Euronext Amsterdam in August 2023 before Euronext listed it as inactive in February 2026 and liquidation proceedings began later that month. Meanwhile, SIX has hosted physically backed crypto ETPs since 2019.

The listing arrives with Bitcoin price hovering near $60,500 after heavy November outflows across U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs.

BIT—formerly known as Matrixport—expanded its Swiss fund footprint after acquiring and rebranding its Swiss asset management arm (originally rooted in Crypto Finance Asset Management).

This approval is a major step for Switzerland, as it allows everyday investors to gain direct exposure to Bitcoin through a regulated Swiss investment fund. It also shows that regulators are becoming more open to Bitcoin as a mainstream investment asset.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) kept leaving crypto exchanges this week as the price of the meme cryptocurrency fell to levels last seen in the spring of 2021, and on Wednesday, the outflow picked up sharply.

According to CoinGlass data, 520.83 billion SHIB left exchanges over the past 24 hours. That amount made up most of the 757.51 billion SHIB that exchanges lost over the past seven days, and over the past 30 days, the outflow reached 2.88 trillion SHIB.

On Wednesday evening, SHIB was trading at $0.00000344, according to CoinGlass. So far this week, the token was down 4.78%, and its market capitalization went down to $2.02 billion, according to TradingView.

According to the weekly chart on TradingView, SHIB last traded at these levels in the spring of 2021, months before the token reached its all-time high of $0.00008845 on Oct. 28, 2021.

From early 2026 until mid-November, the price of SHIB held above $0.000004, and the yearly low stood at $0.00000411 at the July 17 close. In November, SHIB fell to $0.00000373, and in late November, the token dropped as low as $0.00000337. On Jan. 1, the token closed the day at $0.00000692, and since the start of the year, SHIB has lost 50.3% of its value, according to CoinGlass. As of Nov. 22, SHIB had lost 22.7% in November so far, according to CryptoRank.

The latest drop in SHIB came after Bitcoin fell back below $60,000 this week. On Saturday, Nov. 21, Bitcoin dropped as low as $55,150, its lowest price since September 2024. Over the past 24 hours, $57,590 worth of SHIB futures positions were liquidated, and $54,750 of that amount came from long positions on OKX, according to CoinGlass.

The Wednesday outflow was not the first large one this month. On Nov. 17, about 312 billion SHIB were withdrawn from exchanges, according to CryptoQuant. On the same day, the number of SHIB holders on Ethereum passed 1.7 million, according to Etherscan.

CoinGlass data also shows that since late 2024, the total SHIB balance on exchanges has gone down by 19.18 trillion tokens, or 20.54%, to 74.19 trillion, and over the same period, the price of SHIB fell by 88.39%. The remaining 74.19 trillion SHIB on exchanges make up 12.59% of the circulating supply and are worth about $254.75 million.

Most of the 24-hour outflow came from exchanges that CoinGlass groups as "Others," as their combined SHIB balance fell by 88.5% to 70.93 billion tokens. Over the same period, the SHIB balances of Binance and OKX barely changed, and Coinbase, Bitfinex and Bitstamp added SHIB.

As a result, in the week when the price of SHIB fell to levels last seen in 2021, exchanges lost more SHIB in a single day than over the previous six days combined, according to CoinGlass data.

The new accounts follow an October overhaul that brought the firm’s own trading terminal, AI-agent trading, BloFin and static loss limits on every challenge

DUBAI, UAE, November 2026: HyroTrader, a crypto proprietary trading firm, has launched two new ways to get a funded trading account. Hyro Core is a one-phase challenge from $9, and Hyro Instant skips the challenge altogether. Both went on sale on 4 November 2026.

They are the second step of a rebuild that began in October. That month HyroTrader launched its own trading terminal with stock and index contracts and opened accounts on it to AI trading agents. It also added BloFin as a second exchange, made every loss limit static and made its payouts easier to verify on a public dashboard.

Firms like HyroTrader give traders a funded account and pay them a share of the profit made on it. Traders usually earn that account by passing a paid trading test, known as a challenge.

At HyroTrader, every account, funded or not, is a simulated (demo) account running on live market data. The payouts are real money, paid as a share of the simulated profit.

Hyro Instant is the bigger change for a firm that until now funded only traders who passed a challenge.

“Without an evaluation, a firm cannot establish whether a trader has a consistent track record or simply had a few successful trades,” HyroTrader said in announcing Hyro Instant. “Nevertheless, the demand for a faster route is clear.”

Hyro Core is the firm’s lowest-priced challenge. A $2,500 account costs $9, and the largest, $100,000, costs $349. Against One-Step, the firm’s other one-phase challenge, it pairs the lower price with tighter loss limits.

To pass, a trader needs a 10% profit over at least four trading days, with no single day counting for more than 40% of it. The challenge ends if the account loses more than 3% of its starting balance in a day, or 5% in total. Both limits are static, which means they stay fixed to the starting balance and do not rise as the account gains.

Funded Hyro Core traders receive a fixed 80% of the profit as payouts. The fee is not refunded once the challenge is activated.

“A trader’s budget does not necessarily reflect their motivation or skill,” HyroTrader said in announcing Hyro Core.

Hyro Instant, a funded account with no evaluation. Image: HyroTrader

Hyro Instant has no test at all. After identity verification and account setup, the trader receives a funded account with no profit target to reach. It costs from $169 for a $5,000 account to $2,799 for $100,000.

It keeps Hyro Core’s daily and total loss limits and adds a per-trade limit. No single trade may lose more than 2% of the starting balance. A first breach of that trade limit brings a warning, and a second closes the account.

The first payout opens after three qualifying trading days (days on which the trader closes at least one trade above set size and price-move thresholds), with the account in profit. The profit split starts at 80% and can rise to 90% at the firm’s discretion. The fee is refunded only if identity verification is not approved.

Both new accounts run on what HyroTrader built in October. At the centre is the Hyro platform, the firm’s own trading terminal, which needs no exchange account. It offers more than 700 perpetual futures markets (contracts with no expiry date) on live prices. Besides crypto, they include contracts on stocks such as Apple, Nvidia and Tesla, on the S&P 500, and on gold and silver.

Traders who prefer an exchange can instead run any programme on their own demo account at Bybit or, since October, at BloFin. HyroTrader says that in 2023 it became the first crypto prop firm to let traders run a challenge on their own exchange demo account.

On the Hyro platform, Hyro Instant accounts included, traders can also connect their own AI agent through MCP, the Model Context Protocol (an open standard for linking AI tools to other software). The agent places trades for the trader’s own strategy under the account’s usual rules, and the trader can revoke its access at any time.

The October rebuild also made payouts easier to check. HyroTrader lists the payouts it sends on the Solana blockchain on a public transparency page, each with a link to its blockchain record unless the trader has chosen to hide it. In November the minimum payout fell from $100 to $25.

The firm also eased its existing challenges in the same week. One-Step challenges bought from 5 November need at least three trading days instead of five and allow an 8% total loss limit instead of 6%. Two-Step challenges bought from 4 November need four trading days in each phase instead of five.

HyroTrader is a crypto prop firm launched in 2023 and operating from Dubai, UAE. Traders take a challenge or start funded with Hyro Instant, receive 80% of their profits as payouts, up to 90% on some programmes, and are usually paid in stablecoins within 24 hours.

According to HyroTrader’s public payout transparency page, the firm has paid more than $9.5 million in profit splits to traders since 2023, as of November 2026. More than $1.6 million of that went out on the Solana blockchain. HyroTrader says it has funded more than 1,700 traders.

Bitcoin [BTC] witnessed yet another bout of volatility this week that caught the bulls off guard. On Wednesday, the 25th of November, Bitcoin bounced from a low of $57,300 to a local high of $61,622.

This bounce spurred the rest of the crypto market higher too, resulting in $406.85 million in long liquidations and $238.06 million in short liquidations.

The U.S. personal consumption expenditures (PCE) data was released on Wednesday. It rose 3.8% year-over-year, while core PCE rose 3.3% year-over-year.

Headline PCE in line with consensus estimates reinforced the market expectations of a 25-bps Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

A week ago, there was a 6.5% probability of a 50-point rate hike. At the time of writing, this probability was 0%.

It wasn’t bullish news, but it was a catalyst that allowed the price to jump higher and wipe out the dense cluster of short positions that had built up in recent days. Monday’s rally just past $64k was another short squeeze.

As things stand, demand is too weak and pessimism too intense for Bitcoin to mount an immediate comeback.

Founder and CEO of intelligence platform CryptoQuant, Ki Young Ju, noted that there was $16 billion in potential short liquidations from $60k to $100k, compared to just $5 billion in potential long liquidations.

In other words, a short squeeze was much more attractive in these conditions. Notably, a mini short squeeze occurred on Monday, as well as the recent price bounce back above $61k.

The Bitcoin active value to investor value ratio was back near 0.8 after climbing above 1.0 earlier this year, reported a crypto analyst. Moreno. It measures how far the spot price deviates from the True Market Mean, which is the aggregate on-chain cost basis for active investors.

Readings below 1 indicate active investors are carrying losses. Aggregate profitability has deteriorated since the BTC price rebound earlier this year.

The Bitcoin risk index was above 2 and neared its peak value from earlier this year. The metric shows higher readings during sell-offs, when capital turnover intensifies relative to market value.

The two metrics showed increasing stress on the market and offered a more attractive valuation to long-term buyers.

To make a compelling case for a bullish recovery, the selling pressure needs to be absorbed. The evidence at hand does not support sizeable demand- for example, Bitcoin spot ETF flows have been overwhelmingly bearish in November.

This high-tech Huawei home battery pack hopes to hold back Tesla’s latest Powerwall with silicon carbide technology, AI-powered energy management baked in, and enough modular storage to keep even large homes bright and warm when the rest of the block goes dark.

Huawei believes its new Luterra S2 is more than just a home backup battery. The Chinese tech firm is calling it an “all-in-one residential energy system” that combines a hybrid inverter, modular battery storage, and AI-powered energy management in a single, simple, and stackable package that’s available in single-phase versions that put out between 3 and 10 kW and three-phase versions that can push up to 20 kW.

The Luterra S2 is the first system of its kind to use Huawei’s proprietary full-silicon carbide (SiC) architecture, which promises improved efficiency, power density, and ease of use. It’s so easy, in fact, that Huawei claims it can be installed and commissioned in just minutes.

“We are thrilled to introduce Huawei Luterra S2, our next-generation all-in-one residential energy system,” said Steve Zhang, President of Huawei Distributed PV & BESS Business. “By combining full-SiC architecture, AI-driven energy management, and industry-leading safety, Luterra S2 is designed to be smaller, lighter, quieter, safer, smarter and more powerful than ever before.”

Huawei’s basic Luterra S2 configuration starts with “just” 5 kWh of battery energy storage and 3 kW of output. Keeping all that power cool and quiet is a Huawei-developed passive cooling system that does without external fans, keeping operating noise levels below a claimed 29 dB (about the same as my Mac mini). It operates at ambient temperatures from –25° C to about 60° C, and features a sturdy IP66-rated enclosure (safe to hit with a high-pressure hose) with corrosion protection up to C5-M to keep it from rusting away.

#5099. MetaMask Brings Stablecoin Payments to Three Asian Markets With New Card Launch

Home » Blitz news » MetaMask Brings Stablecoin Payments to Three Asian Markets With New Card Launch

MetaMask expands its payment card to Japan, Thailand, and Vietnam for Mastercard transactions.

Cryptocurrency wallet provider MetaMask launched its payment card in Japan, Thailand and Vietnam on November 25, allowing users to spend its dollar-pegged mUSD stablecoin at merchants that accept Mastercard.

The move gives users in the three markets another way to use stablecoins for everyday purchases. Rather than transferring funds to a centralized cryptocurrency exchange before spending them, users can make payments directly through a card linked to their MetaMask wallet.

MetaMask Card uses mUSD, a US dollar-pegged stablecoin, to make payments at merchants that accept Mastercard. Users can pay online with their virtual card or in stores through Apple Pay and Google Pay. At checkout, the required amount of mUSD is converted into the local currency, such as Japanese yen.

In Japan, the card is available only as a virtual version and carries no annual fee. ATM cash withdrawals are not supported. Users can spend up to $10,000 per transaction and $15,000 per day.

Payments made with an mUSD balance at domestic merchants carry no transaction fee, while purchases at merchants outside the user’s country of residence incur a 1% fee.

To apply, users must access the Money tab in the MetaMask mobile app, register an email address and phone number, complete identity verification (KYC), and provide proof of residence.

However, the card does not support direct payments with every cryptocurrency held in MetaMask. Users must first convert assets such as USDC into mUSD before adding funds to their MetaMask Money account.

The Japanese cards are issued by New Zealand-based financial services provider Immersve Limited. MetaMask says its Money account retains a self-custodial structure, allowing users to maintain control of their private keys.

The expansion comes as stablecoin activity continues to grow across Southeast Asia, where digital assets are increasingly used for cross-border payments and transfers.

Chainalysis’s 2026 regional research shows that Thailand and Vietnam, alongside the Philippines, accounted for 14.4% of global small-value peer-to-peer transfers. The report also found that cross-border stablecoin activity exceeded domestic volumes in both countries, reaching $10.4 billion in Thailand and $6.9 billion in Vietnam.

Japan offers a different opportunity. Its developing regulatory framework and growing interest in stablecoins provide another market for MetaMask to test whether crypto wallets can become practical payment tools.

MetaMask first tested its payment card in the UK and Europe in August 2024 before launching it to US customers in February 2026. The service has since expanded to the European Economic Area, Canada, and parts of Central and South America.

#5098. Fidelity Files for Chainlink ETF. What Does It Mean for LINK?

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Fidelity’s Chainlink ETF proposal would hold LINK directly and trade on Nasdaq if it clears the remaining steps. The proposed Fidelity Chainlink Fund, described in a November 25 registration statement, would use the ticker FLNK, although the filing is preliminary and no launch date or final annual fee has been provided.

The larger question is not whether Wall Street can package LINK. It already has. The question is whether Fidelity can attract fresh demand for the token rather than divide the existing market among another set of fund shares.

The proposed fund would hold LINK, not a basket of blockchain companies or derivatives intended to mimic LINK’s price. Its objective is to follow the token’s U.S. dollar performance, less expenses and liabilities. The prospectus identifies Anchorage Digital Bank, BitGo Bank & Trust and Coinbase Custody as custodians, with the trust intending to hold its LINK on Ethereum.

Fidelity also lays out how the price would be measured. Its proposed reference rate uses prices from eligible LINK spot markets, with a volume-weighted median methodology calculated every 15 seconds using rolling 60-minute market data. That is a mechanism for valuing the assets. It is not a guarantee that fund shares will trade at precisely the reported value when markets are thin or volatile.

Nor is this a yield product. The filing states plainly: “The Trust will not stake its LINK.” Shareholders would not receive staking rewards through the fund. They would be buying securities designed to reflect an underlying token’s price, not a wallet balance they can use in Chainlink services.

That distinction matters because the company’s use of Chainlink technology elsewhere is a separate story. NewsBTC has previously reported on Chainlink infrastructure used with Fidelity’s tokenized FILQ fund. An investment vehicle that owns LINK is not evidence of increased demand for Chainlink’s oracle services, and using the network’s technology does not automatically mean buying its token.

This is not the first attempt to make LINK available through conventional securities accounts. Grayscale’s Chainlink Trust ETF, trading as GLNK, had a share creation and redemption program in place from December 2025, according to its SEC disclosures. The Bitwise Chainlink ETF, CLNK, also appeared in a January 2026 Nasdaq information circular.

And fund shares are not the only conventional route. In November, NewsBTC covered Charles Schwab’s rollout of direct LINK trading to eligible crypto clients. These routes do different things, but they establish a useful baseline: access is no longer the same problem it was when crypto products were confined to specialist exchanges.

Fidelity’s possible advantage is distribution. Its name and brokerage relationships may reach customers who would not open a crypto wallet or buy LINK on a trading platform. That is a credible reason the filing matters. But branding, however recognizable, cannot tell investors how much money will arrive once trading begins.

There is also the price of access. The preliminary prospectus leaves the sponsor’s annual fee blank. Until that figure is settled, it is impossible to make an honest cost comparison with competing LINK products. For investors choosing between wrappers around the same token, fees, trading spreads and the gap between share prices and net asset value deserve more attention than a new ticker.

The mechanics are worth getting right. The proposed trust would issue and redeem large blocks of shares through authorized participants, using cash or LINK under procedures described in the filing. Everyday investors would generally trade the shares on an exchange instead of placing orders with the trust.

Those are two different markets. When one investor sells an existing fund share to another, the trade does not by itself require the trust to acquire more LINK. Sustained net creations can increase a fund’s underlying holdings. Redemptions can do the reverse. A rising share price, meanwhile, may reflect a higher LINK price rather than additional tokens entering custody.

That is why the announcement alone provides no evidence of fresh institutional inflows. The Form S-1 is a plan, not a subscription report. It does not tell us how much outside capital will be committed, what portion might come from rival products, or whether investor interest will survive a difficult crypto market.

There is a fair counterargument. Fidelity could appeal to a materially different pool of investors and grow total demand rather than simply redistribute it. The filing establishes a possible channel for that to happen. It does not establish the outcome.

First, the registration statement must become effective and the proposed Nasdaq listing must move forward. The final prospectus should also resolve the missing fee and other commercial details. Those are immediate milestones, not formalities to be assumed away.

If the product launches, the more revealing evidence will arrive afterward: the number of LINK held, changes in shares outstanding, sustained net creations or redemptions, trading liquidity and discounts or premiums to net asset value. Comparisons with existing LINK funds would help separate fresh demand from investors moving between products.

Until those figures exist, the sensible interpretation is narrow. Fidelity wants to sell investors exposure to Chainlink through a familiar brokerage format. Whether that changes the market for LINK is still an open question, and one that a filing cannot answer.

#5097. The Crypto AI Map: Who Does What, and Where Lightchain AI Fits

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Crypto has an AI sector of its own, and from the outside it looks like one trade. Up close, the projects in it do very different jobs, and a comparison only makes sense once you know which job each one does.

Part of the sector already earns real revenue. Venice, a private AI app, became a unicorn in July 2026 with a $65 million Series A, and its CEO, Erik Voorhees, told TechCrunch that the company is profitable, with annualized run-rate revenues of over $70 million. People pay for private AI.

The map goes layer by layer, and each project is described from its own site.

The base layer connects idle graphics cards with the people who need them.

Most of what this layer sells is time on hardware, though Akash and io.net now also sell access to open models through APIs. For teams weighing a rented GPU against their own hardware, Lightchain AI has published a comparison of self-hosting an LLM and a worker network.

Here the network itself decides whose work is best, and pays for it.

This layer competes with ChatGPT on the user’s side of the screen.

Lightchain is building an agents layer of its own, Lightchain Agents, with a waitlist open now.

This is where Lightchain AI sits. It is a layer-1 blockchain built to run AI. Its blog keeps a plain list of what is live on the network today.

Lightchain also touches three of the other layers:

The sector will keep trading as one theme. It works more like a stack, where each layer needs the others: GPUs to run on, models worth running, apps people want, agents that act, and a record that shows what happened. Lightchain’s bet is on that last layer: the more AI runs on open networks, and the more agents pay one another, the more a public record of who served each answer matters.

Lightchain AI is a layer-1 blockchain for AI. Independent operators stake LCAI and serve open models such as gpt-oss, Qwen3, and Llama from their own GPUs. The chain assigns each job, holds the fee in escrow, and keeps a record of every job that anyone can look up. Products live today include Lightchain Chat, Lightchain Desktop (beta), Lightchain Studio, the Lightchain Bridge, and the Lightscan explorer. The LCAI DUNA, a Wyoming association, is the project’s legal entity.

"Sentiment towards Bitcoin can change very quickly. Without Bitcoin changing at all," Webley said on X.

Webley advised investors to consider Bitcoin's movements relative to other assets. Bitcoin's price decline shows investors how much the cryptocurrency has lost in absolute terms.

However, Bitcoin's performance relative to the broader market may indicate BTC is being sold specifically or whether investors are taking profits across multiple markets. Webley did not specify which assets he was comparing Bitcoin against.

"Do I expect Bitcoin to go significantly lower from here? No. But as the past few weeks have shown, predicting short-term price movements is a very challenging task," Webley said.

Some of the most challenging periods for investors, he said, were followed by some of his most profitable periods.

His most definitive prediction concerned Bitcoin's longer-term outlook: "Bitcoin has an incredible future."

In fact, Webley's company has been buying more Bitcoin as its price has been dropping.

On Nov. 17, Smarter Web said it spent around £2.75 million on 55 BTC, bringing its total holdings to 2,905 BTC.

The average purchase price was £49,991 per Bitcoin, roughly 38% below the treasury's overall average purchase price of £81,234 following the transaction.

Smarter Web borrowed around £2.6 million under its Coinbase credit facility to finance most of the purchase. The company used its existing Bitcoin holdings as collateral.

Following the transaction, Smarter Web had around £19 million outstanding under the dollar-denominated credit facility.

#5095. Bitcoin’s Recovery Faces a New Warning After $2 Billion in ETF Outflows

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

The Bitcoin recovery above $60,000 is offering some relief after a brutal November sell-off, but the money flowing through US spot Bitcoin ETFs tells a less encouraging story. The funds recorded more than $2 billion in combined net outflows over four consecutive trading sessions ending November 24.

Bitcoin’s return to the psychologically important price level follows a difficult week in which the cryptocurrency traded as low as approximately $55,300.

The rebound is welcome. What is less clear is whether buyers have returned with enough capital to sustain it.

The scale of the recent withdrawals deserves more attention than the recovery itself.

According to Farside Investors, US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded net outflows of $582.3 million on November 19, followed by another $669.2 million the next day. Withdrawals continued on Monday and Tuesday, bringing the combined total across those four trading sessions to approximately $2.05 billion.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust accounted for roughly $1.77 billion in net outflows during that period.

Wednesday’s figures are still subject to final reporting confirmation, although available data points to further withdrawals.

These numbers do not mean that every institutional investor is abandoning Bitcoin. ETF shareholders include different types of investors, from financial advisers and asset managers to individual traders. Some may be reducing risk, while others could be unwinding positions that were never intended as long-term investments.

What the figures establish is that the ETF market has experienced persistent net redemptions, even after Bitcoin’s substantial decline.

That is not the response bulls would ideally want to see from buyers following a major correction.

Earlier this week, Bitcoin fell below $60,000 again after an initial recovery above $64,000 failed to hold.

Glassnode’s November 24 report, titled The Canary in the Coal Mine, documented the severity of Bitcoin’s latest decline. The cryptocurrency reached approximately $55,300 on November 21, falling beneath the lows established during the summer.

That matters because investors who bought during previous corrections may now be sitting on losses despite having entered the market at what appeared to be relatively attractive prices.

Glassnode’s historical data reveals another uncomfortable detail. Long-term holders recently accounted for more than 75% of Bitcoin’s realized losses before their share fell back toward 50%. Similar periods of selling at a loss appeared during previous bear markets, although that alone does not establish that Bitcoin has reached a bottom.

Their behavior becomes particularly important when Bitcoin starts recovering.

Some holders may use a rebound to reduce their exposure or exit positions closer to their original purchase price. Others may be willing to hold through further volatility. Which group dominates will influence how much buying is required to sustain the next move higher.

A price that previously attracted buyers can become an area of selling pressure when the market approaches it from below.

This is one reason why reclaiming $60,000 should not automatically be interpreted as confirmation that the correction has ended.

There is a credible argument against interpreting persistent ETF outflows as evidence that Bitcoin must fall further.

Markets can begin recovering before investor sentiment improves. In fact, waiting for every major indicator to turn positive can mean missing a substantial portion of a reversal.

Glassnode’s latest research offers some historical perspective. Bitcoin’s realized losses relative to capital inflows over the preceding year have reached their highest intensity since the FTX collapse in 2022. Previous episodes of heavy losses have occurred near major market bottoms, but severe selling alone is not enough to confirm that a recovery is underway.

Bitcoin also trades across a much broader market than US exchange-traded funds. Direct purchases, overseas exchanges and other investment vehicles can absorb selling even when American funds experience redemptions.

The distinction is between evidence that a market can recover and evidence that it has already established a sustainable recovery.

Bitcoin’s latest bounce demonstrates that buyers are willing to step in at lower prices. It does not yet establish whether those buyers can absorb additional selling at higher levels.

If Bitcoin begins to hold its gains despite persistent ETF withdrawals, that would itself be an encouraging development. It would suggest that demand elsewhere in the market is capable of offsetting some of the pressure coming from the funds.

For now, the price and ETF data leave that question open.

Thursday’s Thanksgiving holiday adds another complication to the recovery. US equity markets are closed, removing a regular trading session for American spot Bitcoin ETFs while cryptocurrency exchanges continue operating.

The absence of new ETF flow figures during the holiday should not be confused with an improvement in institutional demand.

With fewer traditional financial market participants active, Bitcoin’s immediate price movements may also provide an incomplete picture of how investors are responding to the recent sell-off.

Friday’s shortened US trading session and the subsequent return to normal market hours will provide more useful evidence.

For traders, the important signals are whether Bitcoin can retain its recent gains, whether ETF redemptions begin to ease and whether buying remains strong enough to absorb selling when normal market participation resumes.

The $60,000 level may dominate the headlines, but the more convincing recovery will be the one that can survive without depending entirely on temporary relief from selling pressure.

#5094. Bitcoin ‘As Important as It’s Ever Been’ if Inflation Rises, Coinbase CEO Says

"Bitcoin investors tend to sell BTC when there's a big IPO. Then they come back."

That's Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong's take on Bitcoin investor behavior, less than a week after the record-breaking $93.5 billion IPO of Claude creator Anthropic.

"Historically, people rotate out of it to take advantage of a big IPO. Then they come back in," Armstrong wrote on X earlier today.

The limited window of opportunity to invest in an IPO helps explain the behavior Armstrong described. For an investor to buy at the IPO price, there's only a certain period during which they can request an allocation of shares. After that, the price is determined by the market.

On Nov. 19, Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq, and that brief window of opportunity mattered.

Shares were priced at $83, up from the $70-$78 range indicated just two days earlier. Anthropic's stock, trading under the ticker ANT, opened at $111.50.

If you bought at that opening price, you paid about 34% more per share than an investor who received an allocation at the IPO price.

When the IPO closed on Nov. 20, 1.127 billion shares had been sold, including 147 million additional shares purchased by underwriters exercising their option.

Of the $93.5 billion in gross proceeds, Anthropic itself received around $91.6 billion. The rest went to existing shareholders.

There was also a separate $26 billion private placement involving investors such as Microsoft, Nvidia, Google and others. In total, the combined transactions were valued at $119.5 billion.

As for the longer-term case for holding BTC, Armstrong's point concerns investors' expectations about the future purchasing power of their money.

"If you think there is going to be more inflation and money printing in the future, bitcoin is as important as ever."

At the heart of the matter is Bitcoin's 21 million supply limit.

If you expect governments to continue expanding the money supply, you may still be excited by the prospect of a major IPO. And you may sell some of your BTC to participate in it.

Armstrong's argument is that the window of opportunity to participate in a major IPO eventually closes.

However, the reasons investors bought Bitcoin in the first place may remain long after the newly listed stock starts trading.

#5091. Bitcoin Mining Difficulty Faces a 9% Jump at the Worst Possible Time for Miners

Strict editorial policy that focuses on accuracy, relevance, and impartiality

Morbi pretium leo et nisl aliquam mollis. Quisque arcu lorem, ultricies quis pellentesque nec, ullamcorper eu odio.

Bitcoin mining difficulty is on course to increase by approximately 9% at the next network adjustment, expected on November 27. The increase would reverse much of the relief miners received less than two weeks ago, leaving operators facing tougher competition for block rewards while Bitcoin trades well below its previous highs.

Current network estimates put mining difficulty at 134.82 trillion, following a 9.13% reduction on November 14. If the projected increase holds, difficulty will climb back toward 147 trillion.

For miners struggling to keep their machines profitable, the timing is hardly ideal. The electricity bill remains largely unchanged, but the same hardware could soon generate less Bitcoin.

Bitcoin adjusts its mining difficulty every 2,016 blocks to maintain an average block production time of approximately ten minutes.

When blocks are produced too quickly, the network makes the mathematical conditions for discovering new blocks more demanding. When production slows, difficulty moves in the opposite direction.

The previous 9.13% reduction in Bitcoin mining difficulty gave active miners some breathing room. Operators could expect to earn more Bitcoin from the same amount of computing power, provided other conditions remained comparable.

The upcoming adjustment, expected at block 977,760, reflects a faster pace of block production during the current difficulty period.

A 9% increase in difficulty does not translate into an identical percentage reduction in mining revenue. Under otherwise unchanged conditions, expected Bitcoin production per unit of computing power would decline by approximately 8.3%.

Consider an operator whose machines currently generate 1 BTC over a given period. Following a 9% difficulty increase, the same machines would be expected to produce approximately 0.917 BTC over an equivalent period.

Nothing about the hardware needs to change for that reduction to occur. The network has simply raised the amount of work required to compete for its rewards.

Mining difficulty only tells part of the story.

A more useful measure of the industry’s financial condition is hashprice, which tracks the expected revenue generated by a given amount of computing power over a day.

Hashprice incorporates Bitcoin’s market value, network difficulty and transaction fee revenue. It provides a clearer indication of whether a miner’s hardware is generating enough income to justify keeping it switched on.

Recent network data from mining industry trackers puts daily hashprice at around $28 per petahash of computing power.

At that level, the economics can become uncomfortable surprisingly quickly.

Consider a hypothetical mining fleet with an energy efficiency of 20 joules per terahash and an electricity rate of $0.05 per kilowatt-hour.

Operating one petahash of computing power continuously would cost approximately $24 per day in electricity alone. Against $28 in gross daily mining revenue, that leaves just $4 before hosting, maintenance, cooling, financing and other expenses.

If difficulty rises by 9% while Bitcoin’s price and average fees per block remain unchanged, that daily revenue would fall to approximately $25.69. The remaining electricity-adjusted margin would shrink to less than $2.

The network adjustment is the same for everyone. Its financial consequences are not.

An operator with newer machines and inexpensive power may comfortably absorb the change. Another running older equipment could find that switching off part of its fleet makes more financial sense than continuing to mine.

The industry’s response to difficult mining economics extends beyond upgrading machines or negotiating cheaper electricity.

Some established Bitcoin mining businesses are redirecting infrastructure toward artificial intelligence and high-performance computing.

Access to substantial electricity capacity, established data centers and existing infrastructure gives certain operators alternatives that smaller mining businesses may not have.

This does not mean Bitcoin mining is disappearing. The projected difficulty increase itself suggests that blocks are being produced faster than the protocol’s target rate during the current adjustment period.

But the growing divergence between mining operators deserves attention.

A Bitcoin mining facility with access to inexpensive energy and efficient equipment operates under a very different set of economic conditions from a business relying on expensive financing and aging machines.

Rising difficulty does not necessarily make the entire industry unprofitable. It makes the difference between efficient and inefficient operators harder to ignore.

The prospect of shrinking margins raises an obvious question for Bitcoin investors: will miners need to sell more BTC to finance their operations?

There is a plausible case for additional selling from businesses facing substantial operating expenses or debt repayments. Mining companies cannot generally settle their electricity bills with anticipated future Bitcoin rewards.

However, network difficulty alone provides no evidence that miners have increased their Bitcoin sales.

Some operators hold substantial treasury reserves. Others sell their production regularly, regardless of market conditions. Businesses can also reduce operating expenses, shut down inefficient equipment or obtain financing instead of liquidating additional holdings.

Actual miner balance data, exchange transfers and company treasury disclosures will provide more useful evidence than the difficulty adjustment itself.

The immediate development to watch is whether the estimated increase materializes at the next adjustment block. After that, hashprice and changes in network computing power will help reveal how operators are responding.

Bitcoin’s protocol is doing exactly what it was designed to do. It adjusts the competition for block rewards without considering whether individual mining businesses can afford to remain competitive.

The machines that become uneconomical have always been the operators’ problem, not the network’s.
