#5057. DOJ Targets 800 Defendants in Largest-Ever Scam Crackdown, Including Crypto Fraud

The U.S. Justice Department said Tuesday that its largest-ever crackdown on scammers has produced actions against more than 800 defendants since March, with cryptocurrency investment fraud run out of Southeast Asian scam centers among its top targets.

The department announced the results of an anti-scam surge that followed President Donald Trump’s Executive Order 14390, signed March 6. Since then, prosecutors have acted in more than 400 cases, bringing new charges, extraditions, guilty verdicts and sentences across 85 federal districts.

U.S. agents also helped police in more than 10 countries raid foreign scam call centers and compounds that targeted Americans. Thirty defendants were extradited to face charges in U.S. courts.

“Predatory scams against the American people will not be tolerated,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said. “The unprecedented results of this surge are just the beginning.”

Crypto sits at the center of much of the effort. The State Department said the U.S. and Southeast Asian law enforcement it funds and trains have helped freeze more than $1 billion in stolen cryptocurrency and take down more than 1.4 million fraudulent websites and accounts.

The Justice Department’s Scam Center Strike Force, formed in 2025 to go after Southeast Asian crypto fraud, says its crypto seizure team has restrained about $1.08 billion in cryptocurrency from these schemes. The team is focused on returning stolen funds to victims.

The FBI’s Operation Blackout has restrained nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, seized more than 14,000 digital devices and helped dismantle more than 29 scam compounds across Asia, Africa and the Middle East, the department said. The FBI also helped free and repatriate more than 2,200 trafficked workers forced to run scams inside those compounds.

“The message to these scam syndicates is clear: if you target Americans, justice will find you,” FBI Director Kash Patel said.

In the past month alone, the Criminal Division filed or unsealed charges against more than 30 scam defendants, including those tied to Southeast Asian scam centers running crypto investment fraud schemes. Other cases involved inheritance fraud, jury duty imposters working from Georgia prisons and sweepstakes schemes aimed at elderly Americans.

The Secret Service said it has restrained more than $200 million in illicit funds during the surge. One of its cases identified a crypto investment conspiracy run from scam centers in Cambodia that targeted at least 174 U.S. victims. In October, a Chinese national was extradited from the Netherlands and arraigned in California over his alleged role.

In Moldova, State Department-backed raids in October shut down five call centers and led to the detention of eight suspected coordinators who allegedly ran fake crypto trading platforms. The SEC said that in the last year it charged three purported crypto asset trading platforms and four investment clubs with defrauding retail investors of more than $14 million.

Homeland Security Investigations said its fraud cases have led to the seizure or freezing of more than $120 million, including funds held in bank and cryptocurrency accounts.

The crackdown builds on months of pressure on overseas fraud rings. Trump planned to highlight the push against overseas crypto scams in October, and the U.S. government seized more than $580 million in crypto linked to Southeast Asian scam networks in February. In October 2025, prosecutors moved to seize 127,271 bitcoin tied to a Southeast Asian scam operation.

The stakes are large. Citing Gallup, the department said 10% of U.S. adults experienced a scam last year, directly or through someone in their household, and Americans lost an estimated $68 billion to scams in 2025, including crypto investment scams.

The department noted that an indictment is merely an allegation and that all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty.

#5056. Crypto bridge hacks can spread losses far beyond the assets they compromise

Recent exploits expose how broken redemption mechanisms, fragmented liquidity and compromised collateral can spread losses across DeFi lending markets.

Multichain’s version of USDC on Fantom was at nearly $0.12 on Nov. 25, more than three years after the bridge that backed it failed, while the Circle-issued USDC and the version bridged to Arbitrum were at $0.9996 each.

Recent bridge exploits at Fusionist and Cyber show how quickly a token can lose the backing or conversion route that held its price close to the original. Buyers can still find a price on a screen even as their options for converting or selling the token shrink.

A bridge lets a token circulate on a blockchain where it was never issued. A US bankruptcy court account describes how Multichain let users lock Ethereum USDC on one side and receive a representation they could later convert back.

In July 2023, Chainalysis traced unauthorized withdrawals that included USDC from Multichain’s Fantom bridge. Multichain announced that bridge service was stopping indefinitely and later said it had ceased operations. On Fantom, the damage reached lender Geist Finance, which stopped operating after taking losses.

On Nov. 25, the USDC version on Fantom was 88.18% below $1, with about $2,472 in reported daily trading volume. Circle-issued USDC and Arbitrum’s USDC.e were both 0.04% below $1, with daily volume of about $15 billion across the native listing and $2.1 million for the Arbitrum wrapper.

CoinGecko quotes (in US dollars) per token at about 18:38 UTC on Nov. 25. Circle-issued USDC and Arbitrum USDC.e were each $0.9996, while Multichain USDC on Fantom was $0.1182.

Source: Circle USDC · · Arbitrum USDC.e · · Fantom USDC

DEX Screener quoted the same Fantom token at $0.04 in SpookySwap’s USDC/WFTM pool, which held about $94,000 in assets, roughly half on the WFTM side.

Eligible Circle Mint customers can redeem native USDC for dollars under Circle’s terms, while Arbitrum’s canonical bridge locks Ethereum USDC and issues USDC.e on Arbitrum.

A holder who converts a bridged token must get the underlying asset back before asking the issuer to convert it to dollars. For specified third-party versions, Circle’s bridged USDC terms make conversion dependent on the available bridge and network.

Georges Chouchani, founder and CEO of Euclid Protocol, told CryptoSlate:

“As long as people believe they can redeem one-for-one, someone will buy the copy at 99 cents and redeem it at a dollar.”

The buyer pockets the difference after fees and other conversion costs, and those purchases can pull the cheaper token toward par. They also depend on the bridge honoring the conversion and the trader being able to complete it.

New York Fed researchers looked at hourly prices for native and bridged USDC and USDT across a selection of networks in the first three quarters of 2024, finding an average correlation of 0.381.

The researchers interpreted the imperfect alignment as evidence that moving value between chains can introduce enough friction to obstruct the law of one price, the idea that equivalent claims should trade at the same price.

Circle reported $3.3 billion of reserves at Silicon Valley Bank in March 2023, and Federal Reserve Board staff found that USDC traded below $0.90 before recovering over about three days.

On Nov. 22, Fusionist’s wrapped ACE fell from about $0.12 to less than one millionth of a dollar in about an hour on BNB Chain, according to Bitquery’s analysis of decentralized exchange trades.

Traders bought the discounted tokens and attempted to convert them back to ACE on Fusionist’s Endurance chain. Bitquery counted approvals for roughly 53.7 million ACE to return and estimated that backing fell to 148 ACE based on the bridge’s BNB Chain records.

Buying a cheap token to convert it would normally pull the prices closer together. In this case, the bridge kept approving conversions after unbacked tokens had entered circulation.

Every completed conversion would take more assets from the vault, leaving less backing for the next holder and making the price gap harder to close.

Gate announced a rollback for ACE/USDT spot trades on its exchange between 17:55 and 19:15 UTC on Nov. 22. Bithumb announced a temporary trading suspension after it had already paused ACE transfers.

On Nov. 24, Fusionist said it was coordinating recovery with exchanges and would share a timeline when it had one. An ACE holder could see a price in a decentralized pool and still face a suspension or potential trade reversal on a centralized venue.

The day before the Fusionist breach, Bitquery traced the issuance of 5,213,000 unbacked CYBER on Solana and the release of the same amount, worth about $1.1 million, from the bridge’s Ethereum vault.

In its Nov. 24 update, Cyber said it had burned an equivalent amount from team and treasury allocations and that the bridge was still temporarily suspended.

The options had already split at Bithumb, where customers could trade existing CYBER balances even after the exchange paused deposits and withdrawals.

“If you have $1 million of liquidity on each of 10 chains, $10 million exists, but a trader on any one chain can only reach $1 million of it.”

What is key for an order is the pool or venue the trader can reach. CoinGecko’s sample showed $33.8 million in reported sell-side depth within 2% for native USDC against USDT on Binance. The same measure for USDC.e against USDT0 on Curve Arbitrum was about $12,231.

Hyperbridge reported an unauthorized mint of about 1 billion bridged DOT. Its initial $237,000 loss estimate covered the immediately visible Ethereum selloff, but after reviewing four affected chains and related incentive pools, Hyperbridge revised the total to about $2.5 million in realized losses.

Chouchani pointed to lending collateral as a route for losses to reach people who never held the compromised token. In April’s Kelp bridge breach, 116,500 rsETH tokens valued at about $292 million were released.

The Aave incident report documented using some of those tokens as collateral to borrow other assets before the protocol froze affected reserves.

If the collateral can no longer be sold for enough to cover the loan, the lending market faces a shortfall. Aave’s report modeled different possible losses depending on how the damage would be allocated.

In this case, the lending market was exposed as soon as it let users borrow other assets against the compromised token, and people who supplied those other assets could bear some of the cost.

Network and contract address help identify who issued the token and which bridge stands between the holder and the underlying asset. Circle’s bridged USDC standard provides a route for eligible deployments to upgrade to native issuance by mutual agreement.

Chouchani said that a design with fewer wrapped tokens can concentrate risk in whatever coordinates settlement across chains. He pointed to smart contracts, validator assumptions, and what happens when one chain takes longer to finalize a transfer.

“No cross-chain design is free of risk, ours included.”

For a specific token, check where the backing is held, whether conversion is operating, and who can use it.

Then check the price available for the amount you want to sell, and what happened the last time trading or withdrawals came under stress.

A token can share the original’s ticker and trade at the same price on a normal day. The contract, conversion terms, and available market tell the investors what that price buys.

In terms of percentage losses, 2022 was overwhelmingly the worst year for Solana. SOL lost 94.15% in 2022. So far in 2026, it's down 43.09%.

SOL declined every month between January and July. August brought a 41.5% surge, followed by another 14.56% gain in September. Then, October and November erased all those gains.

As of Nov. 26, Bitcoin had fallen roughly 21% in November. That provides some context. In October, BTC dropped 7.32%, while SOL lost 19%. Solana was already underperforming Bitcoin before November's losses accelerated.

Meanwhile, another source of demand is faltering. U.S. spot Solana ETFs have recorded $164 million in net outflows over the 30 trading days leading up to Nov. 25.

On Nov. 6, investors withdrew about $24 million from these funds. By Nov. 25, when SOL was trading around $70, the funds recorded zero net inflows. Lower prices had not yet brought ETF investors back in significant numbers.

Solana's network activity actually grew during the summer rally. Quarterly trading volume on decentralized exchanges (DEXs) increased 23% from the previous quarter to $197 billion in Q3.

Of that, a record $7.1 billion came from tokenized equities. That's roughly 3.6% of the quarter's total volume.

Much of the third-quarter growth came from memecoins, according to Bitwise. On Nov. 26, the memecoin platform Pump accounted for $1.29 million of the $2.69 million in daily protocol revenue on Solana tracked by DefiLlama.

For SOL to recover and break even in November, it would need to rise about 34.6% by Nov. 30.

If November ends in the red, even a small decline in December would give Solana a record 10th losing month of the year.

December ended lower in five of the last six years shown on the chart. However, six data points aren't much to base a forecast on.

#5054. Bitcoin’s recovery hinges on a US economic slowdown without a recession

Cooling inflation and resilient employment could ease pressure from the Fed, but deteriorating consumer demand threatens to undermine crypto’s recovery.

Real disposable income for US households rose 0.5% from September, the Bureau of Economic Analysis said in its Nov. 25 income and spending report, and this can impact Bitcoin over the next three months.

Slower inflation could persuade investors that the Federal Reserve has fewer rate increases ahead, while steady hiring and spending could keep them willing to take risk.

If traders expect fewer hikes because they fear a steep economic downturn, demand for Bitcoin could weaken alongside other risk assets.

The October income and spending figures show that personal income rose 0.7% in current dollars, and disposable income rose 0.8% after taxes. The 0.5% real gain measures what that extra income could buy. Real spending fell by less than 0.1%, which the BEA rounded to 0.0% in its table.

In September, real disposable income had fallen 0.2% while real spending rose 0.1%.

October real spending edged down by less than 0.1%. Bars show monthly changes after inflation in the BEA’s Nov. 25 release.

Source: BEA November 25 release · BEA data tables (PDF)

The saving rate was 4.1% in October, as higher private wages and salaries and more dividend income helped lift personal income. One-time Medicare premium rebate payments also contributed. That temporary boost makes it harder to judge how much of October’s gain will carry into future months.

The aggregate spending and income figures can describe the split without telling us whether households saved more because they felt cautious.

The BEA raised third-quarter growth to 4.3% annually from 3.4%, mainly after revising investment and consumer spending higher. The October spending figure offers a first look at a later period, so strong quarterly growth and a weak spending month can coexist.

Headline PCE inflation slowed to 0.3% on the month from 0.5% in September and stood at 3.8% year over year. Core PCE, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3% for a second straight month and 3.3% from a year earlier.

At that monthly core pace, core prices would rise about 3.7% over a full year after compounding. A series of cooler core readings would give investors more grounds to expect the Fed to stop tightening.

On Nov. 5, the US two-year Treasury yield fell 12 basis points, from 4.58% the previous day to 4.46%. Over the same period, Bitcoin fell from $80,420.06 to $76,152.52, about 5.3%, while the Nasdaq Composite fell about 5.5%.

The two-year yield reflects where investors expect short-term rates to go, among other factors. It can fall because price pressures are easing, or because investors see enough economic risk to seek safer assets and expect a weaker economy to limit the Fed’s next moves.

A drop in yields alongside broad selling gives little comfort if investors are cutting exposure to assets that depend on confidence and ready liquidity.

Bitcoin could begin recovering before the Fed finishes hiking, since investors price assets based on where they think rates are headed, so a credible shift toward a lower expected peak or a shorter period of restrictive rates can matter before a policy decision.

Cooler inflation with solid hiring and steady spending would give that shift a firmer footing, while falling yields alongside worsening job and spending data would tell a different story.

The central bank held its target rate at 3.75% to 4% on Oct. 28, with two dissenters favoring a quarter-point increase. In minutes released Nov. 18, almost all participants judged that further hikes would likely be appropriate under their baseline outlooks for inflation and employment.

The Fed’s September projections offer one picture of inflation easing alongside continued expansion. The median participant projection put core PCE inflation at 2.5% in 2027, down from 3.4% in 2026, with the projected year-end policy rate at 4.1% in both years.

The 2027 medians also included 2.4% real GDP growth and 4.1% unemployment. A lower inflation forecast can coexist with rates staying elevated well into 2027, and Bitcoin can respond sooner if the new data lead investors to expect a different path.

If purchasing power continues to grow and spending expands modestly, businesses could face less pressure to raise prices even as demand holds up.

If income gains turn into a surge in spending, inflation could stay high and bring more tightening into view.

If demand falls sharply, the damage to risk appetite could outweigh the benefit of fewer expected hikes. Persistent inflation combined with weakening growth would constrain the Fed and put both sources of pressure on Bitcoin at once.

They can compare that path with what two-year yields and rate futures imply and watch how equities respond.

An orderly moderation in hiring could be consistent with the slowdown Bitcoin needs, while a much weaker report paired with falling equities would give a drop in yields a different meaning.

The Dec. 23 PCE release will show how inflation, purchasing power, and real spending moved in the same month. Together, those readings will help frame the Fed’s next meeting, tentatively set for Jan. 26-27.

If those reports show inflation slowing while jobs and spending hold up, the next test is whether Bitcoin buyers stick around after the initial price reaction. A run of ETF inflows and better spot demand would give a rebound more staying power.

#5052. China’s electric airliner era starts with a 19-seat plane and 400 km of range

COMAC’s CE-25A, China’s 19-seat battery-electric commuter plane, flew with a crew for the first time on Saturday in Binzhou, Shandong. Two pilots and a flight test engineer were aboard the roughly 10-tonne demonstrator, and COMAC says every system worked normally.

It wasn’t the plane’s first flight. The CE-25A had already completed 19 autonomous test flights with nobody on board since February 2, and China’s aviation regulator is now reviewing it for a type certificate.

The CE-25A is a T-tail commuter plane with 10 electric ducted fans on the wings, five per side, instead of propellers. COMAC lists a 300 km/h cruise speed and a 400 km (250-mile) range.

The CAAC accepting COMAC’s type certificate application starts the airworthiness review. It doesn’t mean paying passengers are close, and COMAC hasn’t given a date for commercial service.

The program has been quiet for a long time. COMAC showed a CE-25A model at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai in November 2023, with a placard listing 400 to 500 km of range and a 400 km/h top cruise speed. The full-size aircraft, registered B-0EFH, only became public when photos leaked on Chinese social media on October 28.

The obvious battery candidate is CATL. In July 2023, COMAC, CATL, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University formed a joint venture with CNY 600 million in registered capital to develop electric aircraft, as we reported when CATL launched its aviation unit.

CATL had just unveiled its “condensed” battery at the time, claiming up to 500 Wh/kg at the cell level, and said it was testing the cells to aviation standards. Neither company has confirmed what’s inside the CE-25A, though.

~500 Wh/kg has long been seen as the target for battery energy density to enable electric flight on a commercial scale.

COMAC isn’t alone in flying a large electric demonstrator. In August, Heart Aerospace flew its X1 in Plattsburgh, New York, for 27 minutes. It’s a 25,000-lb aircraft with a 106-foot wingspan, which Heart calls the largest battery-electric aircraft ever flown.

Eviation flew its 9-passenger Alice back in September 2022, then laid off most of its staff in early 2025.

Heart is the closest Western comparison. It dropped its 19-seat ES-19 for the 30-seat ES-30 back in 2022, and the ES-30 now relies on reserve turbogenerators to stretch its range, with BAE Systems working on the battery. Heart is targeting 2031 for service and claims “more than 40%” lower operating costs.

For years, the go-to excuse in the West for doing nothing about emissions was China. Why should we bother, the argument went, if China won’t? Now China is pulling ahead, and it’s doing it by cutting its dependence on fossil fuels.

Look at trucking. Electric trucks hit 50.3% of China’s heavy truck sales in September, and they’re already eating into the country’s diesel demand. In the US, electric models were about 0.3% of heavy-truck sales last year, according to the ICCT.

A great step in the right direction, probably needs a doubling in range but at current rates of progress that will only be five years away.

Now it’s planes, starting where batteries make sense today: short regional routes. The CE-25A’s 400 km shrinks once you keep the reserves regulators require, and a Beechcraft 1900 turboprop in the same class covers well over 1,000 km. So it’s not replacing turboprops anytime soon. But that’s how trucking started too. Short-haul first, then long-haul tractors once the batteries caught up.

And this couldn’t happen fast enough. We’re in the middle of a diesel and jet fuel crisis. Jet fuel averaged $3.50 a gallon in early August, up 63% from a year earlier, according to Heart Aerospace. Every truck and plane China moves to batteries is one less exposed to that.

China also has the batteries to pull it off, with CATL in the joint venture. Meanwhile, Heart has pushed to 2031 and added a fuel-burning backup, and Eviation is a cautionary tale.

If you’re following the electrification of transport, the cheapest place to start is your own roof: home solar can power your EV for close to nothing. #5051. Bithumb Says October Hack Exposed Passports, Bank Accounts and Wallet Addresses

South Korean crypto exchange Bithumb said Wednesday that an October hack of its internal systems exposed more people and far more personal data than it first disclosed, including passport numbers, bank account numbers and crypto wallet addresses.

The exchange also said the intruder had access for about 15 days before being shut out, not the roughly one hour it reported last month.

In an updated notice posted Nov. 25, Bithumb said a follow-up review of the breach of Daou Office, its internal mobile groupware system, turned up additional affected people and additional types of data. The company said the new findings stem from the same incident it disclosed on Oct. 29.

Bithumb now says an unauthorized outside party accessed the groupware system from 1:49 p.m. on Oct. 12 to 3:22 p.m. on Oct. 27, Korea time, and took personal information and files stored there.

That is a sharp change from its first account. Bithumb had said the hack lasted about an hour, from 11:28 a.m. to 12:27 p.m. on Oct. 27, and that it detected the intrusion at 12:14 p.m. that day. The revised timeline means the attacker went unnoticed for more than two weeks.

Bithumb first reported that the data of 6,444 customers and 715 employees, or 7,159 people in total, had been exposed. It did not give an updated count on Wednesday. The notice lists customers, employees of partner companies and current and former staff among those affected.

The list of exposed data now runs to 19 items. It includes member numbers, names, mobile numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, resident registration numbers, passport numbers and driver’s license numbers.

It also covers bank account numbers, home addresses, gender, nationality, copies of ID documents, occupations, employer names and work contact details, as well as transaction histories and wallet addresses. Bithumb said not every item applies to every person, and that affected users will be told individually by email and text message what was taken.

For crypto users, the wallet addresses and transaction records stand out. Paired with names and phone numbers, that kind of data can help scammers target people they know hold digital assets.

Bithumb said Daou Office is an internal business system separate from customer exchange accounts and asset data. It said it has found no sign that its exchange service systems or customer database were directly breached, and that it has stepped up real-time monitoring of unusual trades and withdrawals.

The exchange said it blocked the attacker’s IP addresses, fixed the vulnerability behind the incident and is running a security review of all of its externally exposed services. It has also set up a dedicated support desk for victims that covers financial and legal counseling as well as compensation reviews.

“We will take responsibility for all harm confirmed to have resulted from this personal information breach and provide all necessary support and compensation to affected customers,” Bithumb said.

Bithumb warned users that it never asks for passwords, verification codes or OTP details by phone, text or messenger. It urged anyone who gets such a request to stop responding, confirm through its official app or customer center and report any financial losses to police.

The disclosure adds to a difficult year for the exchange. Bithumb mistakenly credited users with billions of dollars in bitcoin in February, and regulators fined it $24 million and imposed a six-month partial suspension in March over anti-money laundering violations.

It also comes as South Korea weighs new rules for crypto exchanges, including a 20% cap on ownership stakes. Brokerages including Mirae Asset Securities and Daishin Securities have also suffered a series of cyberattacks.

“We are thoroughly investigating the cause of the incident,” Bithumb said.

#5049. US government could be barred from selling its strategic Bitcoin holdings for 20 years

Legislation awaiting House passage would establish long-term holding requirements alongside public verification of Treasury's Bitcoin reserves.

The US Treasury could be required to publicly verify its Bitcoin holdings under legislation advancing through Congress.

The House Financial Services Committee formally reported the amended American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026 on Nov. 24, placing it on the House Union Calendar for the full chamber to consider.

The legislative development follows the committee's Sept. 16 vote, when lawmakers approved the measure 28-21.

Introduced in May by Republican Rep. Nick Begich, the bill would give statutory backing to the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve that President Donald Trump established through a March 2025 executive order.

Under Section 6 of the legislation, Treasury would establish a proof-of-reserves system using public cryptographic attestations and publish annual reports detailing its Bitcoin holdings, transactions, and control of the associated private keys.

Treasury would also appoint an independent auditor specializing in cryptographic attestations to verify the accuracy of its disclosures. The US Comptroller General would regularly review the reserve's management and audits.

The proposed requirements would give investors a clearer picture of how much Bitcoin the federal government has accumulated as a strategic asset.

Trump's executive order required federal agencies to account for their digital asset holdings within 30 days, but directed those disclosures to Treasury and the President's Working Group on Digital Asset Markets rather than the public.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

H.R. 8957 would require a broad internal agency inventory and a public report on Bitcoin deposited in the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve.

The annual public report would detail reserve holdings, transactions and control of private keys.

The bill leaves the cryptographic proof method open. Court and forfeiture records would remain relevant to title and third-party claims.

Maps the roles of Sections 3, 4, 6 and 7 of H.R. 8957, along with the third-party claim process in 21 U.S.C. § 853(n).

The bill leaves the cryptographic proof method open. Court and forfeiture records would remain relevant to title and third-party claims.

The distinction is significant because government-linked blockchain wallets can contain seized Bitcoin that remains subject to legal proceedings or restitution claims. Cryptographic verification, combined with independent accounting, could help establish how much Bitcoin actually belongs to the reserve.

Beyond transparency, the legislation would formalize the federal government's long-term Bitcoin accumulation strategy and limit its ability to liquidate reserve assets.

Federal agencies would have 60 days after enactment to submit comprehensive inventories of their cryptocurrency holdings to Treasury.

The department would then have six months from enactment to establish the statutory Bitcoin reserve and a separate stockpile for other digital assets. Agencies would have another 30 days to transfer eligible holdings.

Federally owned Bitcoin deposited into the reserve would face a minimum 20-year holding period beginning at enactment, during which Treasury could neither sell the assets nor pledge them as collateral.

Two years before that period expires, Treasury would recommend whether to continue holding Bitcoin or begin gradually reducing its position. Potential sales could reach 10% of reserve assets over any two-year period following the lockup.

Meanwhile, the legislation directs the Treasury and Commerce departments to evaluate ways of expanding the reserve without increasing the national debt or imposing additional costs on taxpayers.

The six-month study would examine potential exchanges of other government-held cryptocurrencies for Bitcoin, additional asset forfeitures and partnerships with states, private entities and international counterparts.

However, the legislation faces a tightening congressional timetable. With the 119th Congress approaching its January conclusion, lawmakers have limited time to secure House and Senate approval.

Failure to pass the measure before the current Congress ends would require its reintroduction in the next session, leaving America's Bitcoin reserve governed by executive action without the proposed public auditing requirements.

#5048. XRP Bulls and Bears to Get 3x ETFs Soon

Two proposed U.S. exchange-traded funds would give investors a way to bet on XRP in either direction, with one targeting three times XRP's daily return and the other targeting three times its inverse.

If XRP gains 5% in a single day, the bullish ETF would target a 15% gain, excluding fees and expenses.

If XRP loses 5% in a single day, the bearish ETF would target a 15% gain.

However, investors betting on the wrong direction could lose approximately 15% of their investment in a single day.

The next update is scheduled for Nov. 30. Following a recent amendment submitted to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the registration statements for these ETFs are now scheduled to become effective on Monday.

The issuer has repeatedly delayed the effective date. It remains to be seen whether the funds will start trading anytime soon.

The filing covers a total of eight ETFs, including bullish and bearish funds for Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), Solana (SOL) and XRP.

Even if XRP's price remains unchanged over multiple trading days, both ETFs could record negative returns.

Since the ETFs rebalance daily, it's important to remember that when the price changes direction, the next day's percentage return is calculated based on the investment's value after the previous trading session.

Let's say XRP rises from $2 to $2.20 on Monday and then drops back to $2 on Tuesday. If you hold XRP over these two days, you'll break even.

However, if you invest $100 in the bullish ETF, your position would close Tuesday at approximately $94.55, assuming the fund achieves its daily target and excluding fees and expenses.

If XRP increases by 10% from $2 to $2.20 on Monday, the bullish ETF would target a 30% gain. Your initial $100 investment would now be worth $130.

For XRP to return to $2 on Tuesday, it would need to fall by approximately 9.09%.

The bullish ETF would therefore target a loss of roughly 27.27% on Tuesday. But that loss would be calculated against your $130 position, leaving you with approximately $94.55.

Of course, the bearish ETF wouldn't fare any better.

#5047. Switzerland Picks 57 Countries for Crypto Tax Data Sharing Starting in 2028

Switzerland’s Federal Council has approved 57 countries and territories with which the country plans to automatically share tax information on crypto users starting in 2028, extending its long-standing bank data exchange to bitcoin and other digital assets.

The list includes all European Union member states, the United Kingdom and various G20 countries, the State Secretariat for International Finance (SIF) said in a release on Wednesday. The exchange will run under the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, known as CARF.

With the decision, Switzerland intends to implement the crypto exchange at the same time as other global asset management centers, according to the release. The government did not name the 57 jurisdictions beyond those broad groups, and it did not publish the full list alongside the announcement.

Data will not flow to every name on the list. An exchange will take place only if a partner jurisdiction wants to swap information with Switzerland and meets the conditions of the OECD standard, in particular its requirements on confidentiality and data security.

Before any financial account or crypto data changes hands, the Federal Council will run a targeted check of whether each partner complies with OECD standards. It will rely on a review mechanism Parliament approved on Sept. 28, 2026, which covers both the older exchange of bank account data and the new crypto exchange.

The domestic legal basis for the crypto exchange took effect on Jan. 1, 2026. Earlier this month, though, the SIF said the framework could not be implemented before Jan. 1, 2027, because the partner list still needed approval and notifications had to go to the OECD. The rules do not apply this year.

The Council also approved Armenia and Rwanda as new partners for the exchange of financial account information, with first exchanges due in 2028, and signed off on two notifications needed to carry out the exchange. Both partner lists were broadly supported during public consultations in 2024 and 2025, the government said.

The final list is shorter than first planned. In June 2025, the Federal Council proposed 74 countries relevant to the crypto market, including all EU states, the UK and most G20 members. That plan left out the United States and Saudi Arabia, and it targeted a 2026 start with first data exchanges in 2027.

Wednesday’s release did not say which countries were dropped or whether the U.S. is now on the list. The U.S. has committed to begin CARF exchanges by 2029, according to the OECD’s Global Forum, which lists Switzerland among 27 jurisdictions aiming for first exchanges by 2028.

That U.S. timeline is already shaping policy elsewhere. South Korea pushed its 22% crypto tax back to 2029 partly because it will not receive American crypto trading data until CARF exchanges with the U.S. begin that year. Officials said taxing earlier could put Korea’s domestic market at a disadvantage.

Switzerland’s decision lands as European governments debate how much they should know about crypto holders. On Tuesday, France’s Senate rejected a rule that would have forced bitcoin holders to declare self-custody wallets, while EU states began collecting crypto transaction data under the bloc’s DAC8 directive this year.

For Switzerland, CARF extends a system it already runs for bank accounts. The country has exchanged financial account information automatically under the OECD’s Common Reporting Standard since 2018, ending much of the secrecy once tied to Swiss banking. Its regulated crypto market keeps growing, with the country’s financial regulator clearing its first bitcoin ETF in October.

Under CARF, crypto service providers in Switzerland will have to collect information on users who are tax residents of activated partner jurisdictions and report it to Swiss tax authorities, which then pass it on to those partners once the exchange begins.

#5046. Bitcoin Miners Go 98 Minutes Without Finding a Single Block

Bitcoin miners experienced their longest dry spell since July on Nov. 26. According to Galaxy's Alex Thorn, it took Bitcoin miners 98 minutes and 19 seconds to find the next block.

That's the third time in 2026 that miners have gone this long without finding a block. The wait ended at 18:28 UTC on Thursday.

For anyone trying to get Bitcoin transactions confirmed shortly after the previous block, the gap meant waiting more than an hour and a half.

Even if you paid a very high transaction fee, you would still have to wait until a miner found the next block before your transaction could receive its first confirmation.

Thursday's gap was the 69th longest since 2011, according to Galaxy Research. It was just three minutes shy of the threshold for the top 50.

And this year's other long gap lasted nearly two hours. On July 6, miners took 112 minutes and 26 seconds to find the next block (number 956,953). That was the 19th longest gap on record, according to Galaxy.

Bitcoin automatically adjusts mining difficulty every 2,016 blocks to keep the average block interval at around 10 minutes.

However,  blocks sometimes are found seconds apart. Other times, it takes well over an hour for the next block to be found.

At any given mining difficulty, the chance that a single attempt to find a block will succeed is incredibly small.

If miners have spent 90 minutes trying to find the next block, the chance of succeeding on the next attempt is the same as it was on the first attempt.

So the expected time until the next block is found is still 10 minutes, even if it's already been 90 minutes since the last block was found. That's assuming the network's total computing power and mining difficulty remain unchanged.

Assuming an average block interval of 10 minutes, Thorn said you could expect a gap of at least 98 minutes and 19 seconds about once every 18,600 block intervals.

That means such a gap should occur roughly once every four months, based on an average of about 144 blocks per day.

Galaxy examined 877,290 block intervals going back to Jan. 1, 2011.

Researchers identified 1,948 intervals where at least an hour had passed between the timestamps of successive blocks.

However, Galaxy flagged 97 of those intervals because an adjacent block had a timestamp that was off by at least 10 minutes. This raised questions about the actual length of those gaps.

The longest recorded interval is particularly interesting.

On Nov. 30, 2011, block 155,290 seemingly marked the end of a 144-minute-and-50-second gap.

However, the miner who found the next block had set its timestamp back by 65 minutes.

After excluding apparent timestamp errors, the longest gap was 141 minutes and one second, recorded on Oct. 13, 2011.

#5045. The portfolio risk Toobit’s growth chief wants AI to flag before a trade

Yasser Elmansy describes how leverage can magnify losses when several tokens move together and why the trader should make the final call.

Holding a basket of different tokens often feels like diversification, right up until a market downturn drags them all down at once.

Toobit’s chief growth officer, Yasser Elmansy, told CryptoSlate he’d like an AI assistant to warn traders when a new position adds to a risk they already carry.

For Elmansy, the goal isn’t to hand trading over to bots, but to give retail users better visibility before they click buy.

Trading once required a phone call to a broker; the internet moved it to computers, and smartphones put market access in people’s pockets.

“The internet changed how we execute decisions; AI could change how we prepare for and make them,” he says.

Elmansy imagines an assistant that, with a trader’s permission, could review holdings, open positions, leverage, and trading history. Suppose the trader owns several tokens that tend to move together. The assistant could explain how a single downturn might affect all those positions and how leverage can magnify a loss.

The trader would still set objectives and risk limits, authorize access, and approve consequential actions.

“I’d rather see AI help someone make a better-informed decision than simply push them to trade more.”

Models can misread information or produce convincing but wrong explanations, he warns, and in a leveraged market, small errors can be costly. If many automated strategies react to the same signals, they can worsen volatility.

“Speed isn’t always an advantage if everyone responds in the same way,” he says.

He wants leverage controls and clear ways to pause or stop automation.

That emphasis on informed participation carries over into how Elmansy approaches growth at Toobit. He helps choose partners among trading communities and creators and discusses deal terms. Rather than chasing raw follower counts, he looks at how many people actively trade, how long they stay involved, and how much trading takes place.

He says Toobit already uses those criteria to assess prospective partners.

“I don’t want to attach a specific growth figure to that work without verified reporting,” he says.

The chief growth officer role is recent, he says, so he “wouldn’t claim to have transformed the business in that capacity already.” What has changed is the scope of his thinking.

“To me, sustainable growth isn’t only about why users arrive; it’s also about why they stay,” he adds.

Elmansy’s focus on building durable systems and questioning standard playbooks comes from two decades of learning business and crypto from the ground up.

His first venture started in sixth grade, when he told his brother and a relative he was working in advertising and both asked to join.

“Rather than admitting I didn’t actually have a business, I decided to give them an assignment,” he says.

Armed with a print catalog from a shop his father’s accounting firm used, Elmansy learned that 100 business cards cost about three pounds to produce. He sent his recruits to nearby businesses, including a supermarket, to sell them for 20 pounds.

“To my complete surprise, they both came back with customers and money,” he recalls.

He placed the orders, delivered the cards, and started again. Websites and Facebook ads followed. For years he found the clients and did the work himself, until the business hit a wall because he couldn't scale alone. He convinced a backer to help fund an office and staff, and launched his first marketing agency in 2013, concluding that growth eventually requires trusting people and building structure.

He remembers keeping pictures of Bill Gates and Mark Zuckerberg on that first office wall. He wanted to build his own technology company.

“I wasn’t interested in technology simply as a tool for marketing,” he says.

By 2019, the agency had around 40 employees. When the pandemic hit, businesses cut marketing budgets, so he scaled back and spent late 2020 studying decentralized exchanges and liquidity pools.

After watching an OKX webinar, he contacted the exchange’s recruitment team. He lacked the business development background it wanted, but pitched his marketing and DeFi knowledge and got a chance.

When he joined, his manager mentioned a trading-volume target of $100,000.

“I genuinely didn’t know whether that was large or small,” he says.

What Elmansy did know was influencer marketing. At OKX, he says, he challenged assumptions about what the exchange should pay its partners and argued for backing deals he believed in. He spent nearly three and a half years at OKX, then worked at Pionex, before he joined Toobit in January 2026 as head of global business development.

Looking ahead, Elmansy thinks crypto will reach more people when sending money gets simpler. Today, he says, users still have to think about wallets, private keys, networks, and fees “before they can do something as basic as moving value.” He wants users to understand the risks they take even as the mechanics get easier.

Over the next year, Elmansy says he wants to expand Toobit’s reach and bring the same scrutiny to marketing and product decisions. Getting people to sign up is one part of the job. He wants to understand what keeps them.

#5044. AI agents can pass every accuracy test and still put your money at risk

ShellBench identified 2,589 otherwise correct assistant runs that violated safety rules, challenging conventional measures of AI reliability.

AI assistants can complete complex office tasks correctly while making recommendations that expose users to financial and operational risks.

A new benchmark called ShellBench, released on Nov. 24 by researchers from the OpenClaw Foundation and other organizations, found that 2,589 of the 26,151 runs that satisfied every correctness criterion failed at least one safety check.

That represents a 9.9% safety failure rate among otherwise successful runs, exposing a gap between AI agents' ability to complete assignments and their reliability when handling sensitive responsibilities.

The researchers evaluated 12 AI models across five agent harnesses, the software connecting models to external tools and files, generating 53,100 runs across 100 everyday tasks.

Follow the runs that met every correctness criterion to see how often they still failed on safety.

ShellBench graded correctness and safety separately.

The figures describe rule compliance under ShellBench’s Nov. 24 test design. The severity of real-world harm lies outside the study’s scope.

The upper bar highlights 26,151 of 53,100 graded runs (49.25% by width). The lower bar expands that group and highlights 2,589 of 26,151 (9.9%, rounded to one decimal). Both bars use the counts reported by ShellBench.

The figures describe rule compliance under ShellBench’s Nov. 24 test design. The severity of real-world harm lies outside the study’s scope.

The simulated workspaces contained documents, emails, and spreadsheets, including conflicting information and outdated records that assistants had to navigate to complete their assignments.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

Across all evaluated runs, 8,340 (15.7%) failed at least one safety requirement.

The risks were particularly apparent in a freight invoice reconciliation task, where researchers evaluated whether AI assistants could determine appropriate payments from business records.

According to the research paper, 214 of 531 submissions (40.3%) failed a safety requirement governing payment recommendations.

The failures included recommendations to pay invoices twice, use inflated or incorrect payment amounts, and settle charges outside the appropriate billing period.

Such errors could become expensive as businesses give AI agents greater autonomy over accounting, procurement, and payment processing.

The risks also extend beyond financial transactions. In a separate planning exercise, failing to arrange a child's school pickup was sufficient to trigger a safety failure.

ShellBench's findings raise questions about whether businesses can rely on conventional accuracy and task completion metrics when deciding how much operational responsibility to delegate to AI agents.

Detecting these failures also presents challenges. Researchers used an AI judge to evaluate 90 of the benchmark's 100 tasks, with automated code tests grading the remainder.

The AI judge agreed with human reference labels in 89.9% of 278 individual grading decisions. In a separate reliability test, six of 40 unchanged submissions received conflicting pass and fail verdicts across repeated evaluations.

That inconsistency complicates efforts to automate oversight of AI systems performing sensitive work.

While ShellBench measured simulated mistakes rather than actual financial losses, its findings expose a consequential vulnerability in autonomous AI deployment. An assistant can satisfy every requirement used to establish task correctness and still violate safeguards intended to protect the people delegating that work.

For businesses expanding AI agents' authority from preparing documents to executing transactions, that distinction could determine whether an otherwise successful assignment becomes a financial liability.

#5043. Strategic Bitcoin Reserve Bill Clears House Committee, Heads to Floor

A bill that would write the U.S. Strategic Bitcoin Reserve into federal law is now eligible for a vote on the House floor, after the House Financial Services Committee formally reported it on Tuesday.

The American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026, H.R. 8957, was filed with amendments as House Report 119-894 and placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 789 on Nov. 24, according to congressional records. The committee had voted 28-21 to advance the bill at a Sept. 16 markup.

Rep. Nick Begich, an Alaska Republican, introduced the bill on May 21. It now lists 23 cosponsors, including Rep. Jared Golden, a Maine Democrat, with Reps. Byron Donalds and Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida added on Nov. 24.

The reported text directs the Treasury secretary to set up a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and a separate Digital Asset Stockpile within 180 days of the law taking effect. Bitcoin owned by the federal government would move into the reserve, while other digital assets would go to the stockpile.

The centerpiece is a lock-up. Treasury would have to hold all bitcoin deposited in the reserve for at least 20 years after enactment, and during that period no reserve bitcoin could be “sold, swapped, auctioned, encumbered, or otherwise disposed of for any purpose.”

After the 20 years, the Treasury secretary could recommend selling up to 10% of the reserve in any two-year period. Two years before the holding period ends, Treasury would have to send Congress recommendations on whether to keep holding or begin a gradual release.

Federal agencies would have 60 days after enactment to give Treasury a full accounting of the bitcoin and other digital assets they hold or have seized. Until the reserve is set up, agencies could not sell those coins except for national security, when required by law or a court, or to return assets to crime victims.

The bill also creates a Proof of Reserve system. Treasury would publish an annual report on total holdings, transactions and control of private keys, checked by an independent auditor with expertise in cryptographic attestations, while the Government Accountability Office would provide oversight.

States could choose to store their own bitcoin in segregated accounts inside the federal reserve, keeping title to the coins and the right to withdraw them.

The committee rewrote the bill before reporting it. Begich’s introduced text asked Treasury and Commerce to study funding bitcoin purchases with surplus remittances from Federal Reserve Banks or a revaluation of the Fed’s gold certificates, as well as with tax payments, tariff revenue and gifts.

Those options are gone from the amended study, which now looks at swapping other digital assets in the stockpile, forfeitures and settlements, and partnerships with states or private entities. The amended version also states that nothing in the study authorizes borrowing, pledging government assets as collateral, new taxes or deficit spending to buy bitcoin.

The committee also amended the bill’s title to drop a reference to offsetting costs with Federal Reserve resources, and removed a section that would have required the Exchange Stabilization Fund to report its bitcoin holdings.

Bitcoin Magazine reported on the bill’s bipartisan debut in May and on the full text revealing the 20-year lock-up in June. The reserve itself already exists under Executive Order 14233, signed in March 2025, but an executive order can be reversed by a future president, which is why Begich and his cosponsors want it in statute.

Setting up the reserve has been slow. In July, a report said Treasury and Commerce were competing over who would control it.

Begich’s bill has not received a floor vote. If it passes the House, the Senate would still need to act before it could reach the president’s desk.

#5041. High altitude, bitter cold, zero drivers: autonomous trucks take on Tibetan mine

Finding qualified equipment operators is hard enough for most mining companies, and the extreme weather, punishing conditions, and oxygen-deprived air of the Tibetan mountains combine to make finding operators even tougher for the operators if this high-altitude copper mine – but SANY thinks they have a solution: fully self-driving haul trucks.

Chinese equipment brand SANY has deployed fully 60 of its 70-tonne (~80 ton) payload-rated SKT105ED battery electric haul trucks at the Zhibula Copper Mine in Tibet. Operated by Zijin Minig and Tibet Julong Copper, the mine functions at a dizzying 17,700 foot elevation in a region of the Gangdese Mountains known as the Kailas Range, and the conditions there would challenge the health and safety of even the toughest and fittest operators.

“High-altitude illness becomes increasingly relevant above 2,500 meters,” explains Eacon, in one section of a published paper. “Research involving workers in Andes mines operating between 3,800 and 4,500 meters found that 73% of workers assessed experienced periods of nocturnal oxygen saturation below 85% during their high-altitude shifts, indicating moderate-to-severe hypoxemia.”

That’s bad news for Zijin’s workers – but the good news here, of course, is that the company won’t be needing many heavy haul drivers going forward.

SANY has been working with Perth, Australia-based Eacon Mining Technology to develop an autonomous haulage solution that uses a full suite of both in-vehicle and ground-based sensors, adaptive vehicle controls, and machine learning that can handle the big bad trucks even here in the Kailas range.

“Autonomous haulage offers one way to address this challenge,” continues the Econ report. “Rather than requiring a driver for each truck, autonomous systems allow fleets to be managed through centralized supervision, with personnel overseeing operations and intervening when required. This reduces the need for people to spend entire shifts operating equipment at elevation, while changing how workforce resources are allocated across the mine … depending on the system configuration, some operations can manage autonomous fleets from remote Integrated Operations Centers located away from the mine site, (allowing) personnel to supervise haulage activities from lower-altitude locations, further reducing the need for workers to remain in extreme-altitude environments.”

The working partnership between the two companies combines SANY’s battery-powered truck platform with Eacon’s full technology stack to create dependable, driverless haul trucks with logic and behaviors that are ideally suited to China’s open-pit mining environments.

Eacon technology is currently operating more than 3,100 autonomous trucks cross more than 40 large-scale mines, including Zijin Mining’s Zijinshan Gold-Copper Mine and at the Norton Gold Fields project in Australia.

While specifications for this specific deployment weren’t disclosed, the SANY SKT105E trucks (the “D” is, presumably, the wide-body variant) the company has deployed elsewhere are powered by a dual-motor electric drivetrain, pairing two permanent-magnet synchronous motors with a dual three-speed automated manual transmission. The system delivers 570 kW (~765 hp) of continuous power and up to 820 kW (~1,100 hp) at peak output, with each motor producing some 2,430 Nm (~18,00 lb-ft) of peak torque.

Those motors get their electrons from an absolute whopper of a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery pack in capacities ranging from 423 to 642 kWh, depending on configuration. The big trucks also offer regenerative braking to recover energy on downhill runs, while their fast-charging system can reportedly charge the battery from 20% to 90% in under an hour.

#5040. Bitcoin’s recovery above $60,000 faces a threat from Japan while Wall Street sleeps

Tokyo’s inflation report arrives during the Thanksgiving trading break, potentially reviving pressure on yen-funded Bitcoin positions.

Bitcoin's recovery above $60,000 faces a fresh test from Japan's inflation report while US spot Bitcoin ETFs remain closed for Thanksgiving.

The flagship cryptocurrency fell to $57,210 on Wednesday before recovering to close at $60,368, according to CryptoSlate's data. Bitcoin extended those gains modestly on Thursday, trading around $60,538 as of 10:40 UTC.

However, the recovery comes as Bank of Japan officials signal that further monetary tightening may be necessary to contain inflation.

Speaking in Yamanashi on Thursday, BOJ board member Naoki Tamura said the central bank could accelerate interest rate increases if underlying inflation shows signs of exceeding its 2% target.

Tamura also reaffirmed his estimate that Japan's neutral interest rate, the level at which monetary policy neither stimulates nor restrains economic activity, stands at around 2%. That is 75 basis points above the BOJ's current overnight policy rate of 1.25%, which the central bank maintained at its October meeting.

The yen strengthened modestly on Thursday, with BOJ data showing the dollar trading around 159.17 yen at 5 p.m. in Tokyo, compared with 159.21 earlier in the day.

Markets will get a fresh read on Japan's inflation trajectory when Tokyo publishes its preliminary November consumer price figures at 8:30 a.m. local time on Friday, equivalent to 6:30 p.m. ET on Thanksgiving.

The release precedes Japan's nationwide inflation report on Dec. 18, giving investors an earlier opportunity to reassess expectations for BOJ monetary policy.

That timing leaves Bitcoin exposed to changes in those expectations before US spot ETFs resume trading during Friday's shortened NYSE Arca session.

Japan's monetary tightening poses two distinct risks to investors who borrowed yen to finance positions in Bitcoin and other dollar-denominated assets.

The strategy, commonly known as the yen carry trade, involves borrowing in Japan's relatively low-interest-rate currency and deploying the proceeds into assets elsewhere in pursuit of higher returns.

A strengthening yen increases the dollar cost of repaying that debt for investors who have not hedged their currency exposure, eroding returns even when Bitcoin's price remains unchanged.

Higher Japanese interest rates compound that pressure by potentially increasing the cost of refinancing existing positions.

Together, those developments can make leveraged investments less profitable, encouraging traders to reduce exposure to risk assets to repay their yen-denominated liabilities.

Japan's two-year government bond yield provides another indication of how investors are pricing the country's monetary policy outlook. A rise in short-term yields alongside a strengthening yen following Friday's inflation report would signal mounting pressure on yen-funded positions.

Conversely, softer inflation could temper expectations of accelerated BOJ tightening, easing one potential source of selling pressure on Bitcoin.

The immediate risk is that a hotter inflation reading could renew pressure on Bitcoin's fragile recovery while US spot ETF trading remains suspended. Those funds will reopen at 9:30 a.m. ET on Friday, approximately 15 hours after Tokyo's inflation release, leaving Bitcoin's continuously operating global markets to absorb the initial reaction.

#5036. OpenAI’s Codex helps amateur astronomer uncover two possible planets NASA’s data had missed

A SETI Institute astronomer independently recovered both signals after an OpenAI engineer used AI-generated software to search observations of 100,000 stars.

An AI-assisted search of NASA's archived telescope data has uncovered two possible planets, with preliminary checks by a professional astronomer recovering both signals.

In a Nov. 24 report, OpenAI detailed how two amateur astronomers used its Codex and Astra tools to search observations of millions of stars for previously overlooked planetary candidates.

Kevin Bond, an OpenAI engineer, used Codex to develop software that detects recurring declines in stellar brightness, a potential indication of a planet passing in front of its host star.

Bond combined existing detection methods into a program that deployed two AI agents. One identified promising signals, while the other subjected those findings to further examination.

Running the software against archived observations of approximately 100,000 stars from NASA's Kepler Space Telescope produced more than 200 signals, including 10 associated with previously confirmed planets.

Vishal Gajjar, an astronomer at the SETI Institute, independently recovered two of Bond's findings.

The first involved a relatively cool star, KIC 5689121, whose brightness declined every 13.8 days. OpenAI said the signal was consistent with a potential planet approximately 2.4 times Earth's diameter. The second, KIC 6691030, exhibited recurring dips every 4.8 days, suggesting a potential planet smaller than Neptune.

OpenAI says SETI Institute astronomer Vishal Gajjar recovered both dips in the same Kepler data Kevin Bond searched.

Each repeat interval gives astronomers a pattern to test in follow-up observations.

The traces illustrate timing with schematic dip shapes and depths. The causes of both dips remain unresolved.

“Our initial checks are encouraging, and follow-up observations will tell us more.”

While Bond focused on Kepler's archived observations, another amateur astronomer, Ethan Byrd, used OpenAI's Astra to examine telescope data covering approximately 19 million stars.

Byrd developed two searches, including one targeting planetary candidates within habitable zones, where atmospheric conditions could allow liquid water to exist on a planet's surface.

His initial search identified 49 candidates. Byrd has submitted one to researchers working on NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission, and two others are awaiting submission.

Astronomers have used artificial intelligence to identify planets for years. In 2017, NASA announced the discovery of Kepler-90i using a neural network trained to recognize planetary signals in telescope observations.

General-purpose AI tools now let amateur astronomers develop their own detection software and search vast archives for signals earlier searches may have missed.

However, recurring declines in stellar brightness can also result from eclipsing stars or fluctuations in telescope instruments.

Astronomers could investigate Bond's candidates by observing their host stars at the predicted transit intervals and measuring whether gravitational forces from potential orbiting planets cause detectable stellar movement.

Establishing whether either signal represents an undiscovered planet could take months or years, OpenAI said.

#5035. Mowing milestone: Greenzie surpasses 255,000 autonomous miles mowed

Autonomous lawncare specialists Greenzie passed a major milestone with their self-driving mowers last week, surpassing 255,000 cumulative robomowing miles. For context, that’s far enough to mow every inch of space between the Earth and Moon.

Greenzie announced the self-driving milestone last week, and it’s genuinely impressive, reflecting Greenzie Powered Autonomy mowing more than 9 billion (with a b) square feet of turf across more than 200 commercial customers, 45 US states, and more than 500,000 equivalent man-hours of mowing.

And, while I might have pointed the fact that Greenzie mowers have covered more miles in its press release than Daimler’s entire hydrogen truck fleet, the company really seems to be leaning into the Moon angle.

“We mowed to the moon, but the real achievement is the commercial experience behind those miles,” says Charles Brian Quinn, co-founder and CEO of Greenzie and almost definitely the guy who first came up with the lunar lawncare line. “Every mile represents equipment working on real properties with commercial crews. That experience has shaped our technology, strengthened our OEM partnerships and taught us how to help customers successfully integrate autonomy into their daily operations.”

Greenzie develops autonomous packages for, and maintains OEM relationships with electric brands Mean Green Electric Mowers (whose Vanquish Autonomous commercial mower is shown, above), and Greenworks Commercial, as well as gas-powered brands like Bobcat and Wright Manufacturing. Regardless of what powers the mowers, Greenzie supplies the self-driving technology and integration expertise, while its OEM partners develop and manufacture the equipment that does the actual cutting, clearing, and whatever else their clients need.

“Successful autonomy requires more than capable technology,” said Steve Bush, chief operating officer of Greenzie. “Customers need to understand where autonomy fits into their operations, how to prepare their crews and how to measure success. We have spent years learning those lessons alongside our customers and OEM partners, creating a more consistent path to adoption as the industry grows.”

The Mean Green Vanquish Autonomous featured gere is a fully electric, stand-on, zero-turn (ZTR) mower built around an all-day-ready 22 kWh li-ion battery pack and featuring a 60″ rear-discharge mulching deck.

Mean Green claims that the combination of big battery and the electric motors that drive the ZTR mower and spin up its blades are good up to eight hours of continuous mowing on a charge, with an aluminum chassis and deck helping to keep the machine’s overall weight down for easier towing maximum efficiency.

The company says the mower can operate in either manual or autonomous mode, with Greenzie’s self-driving software supported by six depth-sensing stereo cameras providing 360-degree vision, RTK-corrected GPS, and visual-inertial odometry for onboard site mapping and precise positioning, which Greenzie says allows the mower to detect obstacles up to twenty feet away, recognize designated keep-out zones, and automatically return to its starting point when called back.

A top speed of 11.5 mph and the ability to repeat saved mowing routes, the Vanquish is designed to give commercial landscaping crews another productive worker without adding another person to the payroll … which, with a $60,000 asking price, is money they will probably still need.

Let’s get some pro-labor rage going in the comments, and don’t forget to mention what kind of paycheck you’d need to get to go work in landscaping 2,000+ hours a year while you’re there.

#5032. Walmart’s Black Friday rollout reveals how AI agents could spend money without controlling your wallet

Spending limits, restricted payment access and single-use authorization tokens underpin the retailer’s approach to autonomous commerce.

Walmart is allowing shoppers to purchase Black Friday deals through Meta’s AI assistant Muse without sharing their saved card details.

The retailer announced the integration on Nov. 24, expanding its Agent Gateway to allow customers to discover products, build shopping carts, and complete purchases through conversations with Meta’s AI assistant.

Shoppers can ask Muse to find television deals, identify discounted products available for delivery or recommend items based on their preferences. Walmart handles product discovery and checkout through its Gateway, which connects external AI assistants to the retailer’s shopping infrastructure.

To make purchases, shoppers must link their Walmart accounts through a sign-in process that redirects them to the retailer before returning them to Muse.

When adding an item to their cart for the first time, shoppers establish an Agent Profile within their Walmart account and set a spending limit for the assistant.

The profile allows customers to distinguish AI-assisted purchases from other orders in their purchase history. They can also revoke the assistant’s purchasing authority by deleting the profile.

Walmart retains control of payment processing. Under its Agentic Access Terms, only shoppers can designate which saved payment method an AI assistant can use. External agents cannot add cards, change payment preferences or access raw card details, including full card numbers.

Instead, each transaction requires a short-lived authorization token tied to the merchant, shopping cart, purchase amount and session. The token expires upon use, requiring fresh authorization for subsequent transactions.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

Walmart matches requests from Muse. The shopper manages spending and payment permissions in their Walmart account.

Shoppers check out inside Muse with a saved Walmart card. Walmart says outside agents receive no raw saved card details.

Walmart’s announcement leaves the exact Muse approval prompts and eligible locations and devices unspecified. The diagram depicts responsibilities and the shopping request.

The illustration shows the shopping request and the shopper’s account controls described by Walmart in the November Muse walkthrough and the payment provisions in its Gateway terms.

Walmart’s announcement leaves the exact Muse approval prompts and eligible locations and devices unspecified. The diagram depicts responsibilities and the shopping request.

The integration builds on Walmart’s Agent Profiles, introduced in October as part of its efforts to give customers greater control over purchases made through AI assistants.

By default, shoppers must approve purchases initiated by an agent. However, they can authorize assistants to complete transactions independently within a predetermined spending limit.

Walmart can still request additional confirmation even when a purchase falls within that limit. Its terms also allow the retailer to intervene when transactions exceed or conflict with a customer’s purchasing preferences.

The arrangement creates a framework for AI assistants to move beyond product recommendations and execute purchases on behalf of consumers without directly controlling their payment credentials.

However, Walmart’s launch announcement did not specify when shoppers using Muse would encounter additional approval requests after granting an assistant purchasing authority.

The retailer plans to extend its Gateway to more applications and AI assistants, potentially expanding the number of platforms through which customers can authorize purchases.

Walmart’s existing return policy applies to purchases completed through Muse, although the company has yet to specify which locations and devices are eligible for the rollout.

#5030. Is Tesla rushing out a half-baked Cybercab just to shave MKBHD’s head?

Elon Musk called YouTuber Marques Brownlee “a chicken” early Saturday, hours after Tesla opened invite-only Cybercab orders at $29,990 and Brownlee argued that his famous head-shaving bet isn’t lost.

Tesla has about seven weeks to get a Cybercab into a customer’s hands for under $30,000 before 2027, but the half-baked version of Cybercab that they opened orders for with delivery in December makes it look like it’s just to win this dumb bet.

Surely Tesla isn’t down enough to deliver a half-baked product just to “prove” a YouTuber wrong? Or is it?

After Tesla’s “We, Robot” event in October 2024, Brownlee (MKBHD) said there was no way Tesla would deliver a Cybercab to a customer for $30,000 or less before 2027. If it did, he’d shave his head on camera.

Musk has taken it personally ever since. When the first Cybercab came off the Giga Texas line in February, he replied “Gonna happen 😂” to a bald-MKBHD meme, which we covered at the time. In September, after Brownlee doubled down in a new video, Musk wrote: “I guess he really wants to shave his head 🤷‍♂️”

On Friday, Tesla started inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use. The order page lists $29,990, a mandatory $299 per month Autonomy Subscription, a $1,000 non-refundable deposit, and an estimated delivery of December 2026, only in Tesla’s Texas Robotaxi cities.

As we reported Friday, the car only operates inside Tesla’s Robotaxi geofences. And Tesla’s Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement says it “will not operate” without the $299 plan, bans owners from putting it on the Robotaxi network or using it for ride-hailing, and lets Tesla shrink the operating area at any time.

So Tesla designed a robotaxi, then offered it to select private owners who aren’t allowed to use it as a taxi. Over five years, that’s $47,631 before insurance, registration, and charging. And you are limited to small geofenced areas. If you stop paying Tesla’s monthly fee, which it can change at all times, your cybercab becomes a paperweight.

Brownlee laid out his case Friday night. There are no deliveries yet, the car is invite-only rather than publicly available, and it can’t be used as a cab outside of the existing geofences. He called it “a paperweight if I take this thing home,” though he admits that last point isn’t technically part of the bet.

The memes are everywhere, so let’s go back over the bet: Cybercab publicly available for under $30k by the end of 2026My hair is safe for several reasons1: No deliveries yet. But they’re estimating starting in December so that’s neat2: Invite only, not actually publicly… https://t.co/NCD2aFbe2c

Tesla fans fired back with clips from his September video, where he described a car that “will not ship to regular people like you and me for $30k before the end of 2026.” Whole Mars Catalog, an Elon Musk propagandist whose real name is Omar Qazi, told him to “be a man and honor your word.” Musk reposted it, then replied:

Musk also reposted a Grok answer claiming the current offer “matches” the conditions of the bet.

But around the same time, Musk replied directly to Brownlee’s post about the order page, and it didn’t help Tesla’s case:

“It will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval. But the monthly fee is too high. Should match the cost of Tesla FSD and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.”

That’s Tesla’s CEO confirming, a day after launch, that the car can’t be sold outside the areas where it already operates and that its price is wrong. A price that Musk fully controls.

Yes, it looks like Tesla is rushing this out just to win a bet against a Youtuber. Absolutely insane behavior. We’ve seen this movie before. In June 2025, Tesla did a single “autonomous delivery” of a Model Y to meet a Musk deadline, then never did it again.

Tesla always pitched the Cybercab as a vehicle for its Robotaxi network. Now, seven weeks before the deadline, a personal-use version shows up that’s invite-only, Texas-only, banned from doing the one thing it was designed for, and attached to a subscription Musk himself says is too expensive. If you set out to build a product whose main job was letting Musk claim he won a Twitter bet, it would look a lot like this.

This Cybercab offering is completely broken. The value proposition is awful. As others have put it, it’s a permanent variable rate lease starting at $300 a month with a ridiculous $30,000 down payment.

Besides, the bet was "under 30k." Starting price is under 30k, but a subscription is required, which takes it over 30k, just to use it for one day. They could have given the car away for free, and just charged a fee to use it. Doesn't change the total cost.

What do you get for this deal? A 2-seater vehicle that only works in small, incomplete, geo-fenced areas and has no steering wheel to do anything else with it. Meanwhile, Tesla insists that the Model Y, like the ones used in its current Robotaxi service alongside the Cybercab, uses the same self-driving technology.

You can buy one for $40,000, and you get a lot more car than the Cybercab; then you can pay $99 a month for FSD instead of $300 a month. Tesla is supposed to let current Tesla owners drive without supervision in the geo-fenced areas, which would basically be the same product as what Tesla is offering right now with the Cybertruck, but you are not a slave to Tesla, which can brick your car at any time or change the terms.

This offer simply makes no sense, and Musk is sort of admitting it by saying the price should be the same as FSD, not $300 a month.
