#5028. Bitcoin’s $60,000 recovery masks a growing threat that could push its price as low as $29,000

Galaxy Research says Bitcoin has exceeded historical bear market timelines while failing to meet 11 of its 13 historical bottom indicators.

Bitcoin recovered above $60,000 after slipping below that mark on Nov. 25, in a volatile week in which Bitcoin fell to around $55,000, its lowest level since September 2024.

BTC rebounded to $63,000 on Monday, but subsequently surrendered much of those gains.

According to Talos, Bitcoin lost 7.9% over the week, compared with declines of 2.9% for the S&P 500, 4.5% for the Nasdaq 100 and 7.8% for gold. Over 30 days, Bitcoin has fallen 25.3%, approximately 2.6 times the Nasdaq 100's decline.

Bitcoin's correlation with traditional risk assets has also strengthened. Its 30-day correlations with the S&P 500, Nasdaq 100 and Nvidia climbed to 0.78, 0.77 and 0.68, respectively, roughly 1.4 to twice their one-year medians.

Galaxy Research noted that Bitcoin's recent struggles are particularly unusual given its September recovery above the 50-week moving average, which has historically helped identify the end of bear markets.

Bitcoin has since fallen below both its 50-week and 200-week moving averages, breaking a recovery pattern that had held since 2011.

Bitcoin reclaimed its 50-week moving average in September after spending 44 consecutive weeks below it. It held above the indicator for seven weeks, reaching a daily close of $86,521 on Oct. 4, nearly 48% above its June low.

Galaxy found that none of the seven previous recoveries that sustained the moving average for at least seven weeks later produced a new bear-market low, even intraday.

September's recovery differed from earlier instances in one significant respect. Previous recoveries after prolonged periods below the moving average followed declines of 76.7% to 92.7%, whereas September's followed a comparatively shallow 53% drawdown on a closing basis.

Bitcoin's subsequent decline to $55,100 on Nov. 21 prompted Galaxy to withdraw its October assessment that the bear market ended in June.

The breakdown shifts attention to Bitcoin's June 30 closing low of $58,525.

Galaxy identified seven completed instances in which Bitcoin closed below a bear market low that had held for at least 60 days and from which the cryptocurrency had rebounded at least 20%.

All seven resulted in further declines of at least 17.1%, with a median loss of 51.8%. Applied to Bitcoin's June closing low, those historical outcomes would put the cryptocurrency at approximately $48,500 and $28,200, respectively.

However, another closing low would push Bitcoin beyond the historical duration of its bear markets.

As of Nov. 22, 412 days had elapsed since Bitcoin reached its record closing price of $124,824 in October 2025. Its four previous bear markets took between 163 and 406 days to bottom.

The current downturn has also exceeded historical halving-to-bottom timelines. The three previous cycle lows occurred between 777 and 912 days after their respective halvings, compared with the 946 days since Bitcoin's April 2024 halving.

While those timelines suggest Bitcoin is overdue for a recovery, its valuation and investor behavior point toward an unfinished bear market.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

Bitcoin's previous four bear markets recorded peak-to-trough closing-price declines of approximately 93%, 85%, 84% and 77%, respectively.

Successive downturns have become shallower, but the largest reduction between previous cycles was eight percentage points. A bottom at the June closing low would represent a 24% reduction.

The divergence extends to Bitcoin's realized price, which estimates the aggregate cost basis of its circulating supply.

During previous bear markets, Bitcoin spent between 140 and 304 days below its realized price. It has yet to register a single daily close below that level, which stood at $53,205 on Nov. 22.

Meanwhile, the proportion of Bitcoin's supply held at a loss reached 57% on Nov. 20, within the 55% to 61% range recorded at previous cycle bottoms.

Despite that financial distress, Bitcoin's 30-day realized losses peaked at just 3.6% of its realized capitalization in February, compared with peaks of 7.3% to 16.7% during previous bear markets.

Investor sentiment has deteriorated more sharply. Galaxy's proprietary Bitcoin Fear & Greed Index fell to 5.2 on Nov. 21, its lowest reading since June 2022 and among the lowest 0.5% of historical readings.

Yet the index has spent just six days at or below 10 during the current downturn, compared with between 12 and 57 days during previous bear markets, including the month following their bottoms.

Derivatives traders have also maintained relatively resilient positioning. Bitcoin perpetual futures funding averaged a positive annualized rate of 4.3% over the seven days through Nov. 22, compared with negative 24.5% shortly after the November 2022 bottom.

As of Nov. 22, Bitcoin satisfied just two of the 13 historical bottom indicators Galaxy tracks.

The conflict between BTC's historical cycle duration and the depth of its losses leaves Galaxy examining two potential scenarios.

If cycle timelines prevail, several valuation measures point to potential support between $48,400 and $53,200. These include Bitcoin's realized price, its long-term holder cost basis, and the smallest historical decline following the breakdown of an established bear market low.

A bottom within that range would still represent Bitcoin's shallowest bear market on record.

However, a return to the valuation extremes that characterized previous downturns could push Bitcoin toward levels between $29,100 and $46,100.

Galaxy is also monitoring US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded products, which have shed 71,339 BTC worth $4.95 billion since October. Their holdings have declined to approximately 1.24 million BTC, just 1.5% above their July trough.

A break below that 1.22 million BTC trough, alongside a weekly close below Bitcoin's realized price, would strengthen the case for a deeper downturn.

Conversely, reclaiming the 200-week moving average at $68,159 and subsequently the 50-week average at $74,401 would move Galaxy back toward its October recovery thesis.

#5025. Volkswagen prices its new ID. Cross for the UK, but the $35,000 version comes later

Volkswagen revealed how much its new ID. Cross will cost, with prices starting at around $35,000 in the UK. But if you’re hoping to get the cheaper version, you’ll have to wait a bit longer.

After opening orders for the ID. Cross in Europe in July, Volkswagen is preparing to launch the entry-level electric SUV in the UK.

The ID. Cross is the all-electric equivalent of the T-Cross, Volkswagen’s smallest and most affordable SUV in Europe and the UK.

Following the ID. Polo, the ID. Cross is the latest from Volkswagen’s electric urban family of compact cars.

The electric SUV is 4,153 mm long, about the same length as the T-Cross, but its dedicated MEB+ platform offers more interior space. It seats five and offers a 475-liter boot, 20 liters more than the gas-powered T-Cross with the rear seats pushed all the way forward.

When the rear seats are folded, the electric ID. Cross offers up to 1,345 liters of overall luggage volume.

Like in Europe, the Volkswagen ID. Cross will be available with two battery packs in the UK: a 37 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) pack and a 52 kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) pack.

The ID. Cross with the larger 52 kWh battery offers up to 265 miles of WLTP range, while the 37 kWh version provides up to 194 miles of WLTP range.

With DC fast charging of up to 105 and 88 kW, Volkswagen said the vehicle’s battery can charge from 10% to 80% in as little as 23 minutes.

All versions are equipped with vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities, allowing it to be used as a mobile power bank for an e-bike, campsite, or other external electronic devices.

Inside, the ID. Cross adopts VW’s revamped interior digital cockpit design. Cross adopts VW’s revamped interior digital cockpit design. The setup includes a 10.25″ Digital Cockpit Pro instrument display and a 12.9″ infotainment screen. Based on driver feedback, Volkswagen brought back physical buttons for climate control and other vehicle functions.

Volkswagen will open orders for the ID. Cross Life and Style trims in the UK with the 52 kWh battery and 208 hp (211 PS) motor will go on sale on Thursday, November 19, starting at £30,260 ($40,000) and £33,675 ($44,500), respectively.

The base ID. Cross Life and Style trims with the 37 kWh battery will go on sale in January 2027, with prices starting at £26,985 ($35,500) and £30,400 ($40,100).

Volkswagen said the 52 kWh version is eligible for the UK government’s £1,500 ($2,000) electric car grant. Eligibility for the 37 kWh versions is expected to be confirmed soon.

In Europe, Volkswagen opened orders for the entry-level ID. Cross Trend last month, starting at €27,995 ($31,000) in Germany, including VAT.

As the electric counterpart to its popular T-Cross, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said the ID. Cross is “modern, reliable, and above all, affordable.”

Sadly, VW has no plans to bring the ID. Cross to the US. In early 2027, it will launch the new ID. Tiguan, which will replace the outgoing ID.4 SUV.

#5023. Chainlink jumps 10% as its Wall Street ambitions gain momentum on two fronts

Fidelity is expanding investment access to LINK as Chainlink develops the infrastructure to keep tokenized financial markets operating around the clock.

Chainlink's LINK token climbed 10% over the past 24 hours to $9.20 as the network deepened its integration with traditional finance.

The rally comes as Fidelity Investments filed to launch a spot Chainlink exchange-traded fund (ETF), a day after enabling direct LINK trading on its cryptocurrency platform.

Meanwhile, Chainlink has expanded its financial market data infrastructure to support round-the-clock trading and lending involving tokenized stocks, commodities and other real-world assets, including during market holidays such as Thanksgiving.

On Nov. 25, Fidelity submitted a registration statement to the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) for its proposed Fidelity Chainlink Fund, which would trade on Nasdaq under the ticker FLNK.

The fund would hold LINK directly, with Anchorage Digital, BitGo and Coinbase Custody safeguarding its assets. It would support cash and in-kind share creations and redemptions but would not stake its underlying tokens.

The filing came a day after Fidelity added LINK, AAVE and UNI to its Fidelity Crypto platform, expanding its customers' access to digital assets.

While eligible Fidelity Crypto customers can now purchase LINK directly, the proposed ETF would extend that access to investors seeking exposure through conventional brokerage accounts.

The consecutive moves could substantially broaden LINK's investor base. Fidelity serves approximately 57 million individual investors and reported $7.9 trillion in managed assets and $20.1 trillion in assets under administration at the end of September, making it one of the largest financial services firms in the US.

However, Fidelity is entering a market where investor appetite has weakened considerably.

According to SoSoValue data, Grayscale and Bitwise's spot Chainlink ETFs have attracted $176 million in cumulative net inflows since their respective launches. However, the funds recorded net inflows for just one day in November, putting them on course for their first month of net withdrawals since the market's inception.

Daily net flows for GLNK and CLNK through Nov. 25. Values follow Maketo's displayed rounding and totals are approximate, and non-trading days are excluded.

The slowdown in demand, coupled with LINK's price decline, has reduced the funds' combined net assets by approximately 33%, from $238.2 million at the end of September to $158.6 million on Nov. 25.

Fidelity's extensive retail and financial advisory network could help revive demand, but limited fresh capital could also intensify competition among issuers.

With Fidelity yet to disclose its management fee or launch date, the terms of its offering could determine how effectively it competes with Grayscale and Bitwise for LINK investors.

Beyond expanding investment access to LINK, Chainlink is positioning its infrastructure to capture growing demand for financial markets that operate outside traditional exchange hours.

On Nov. 26, the decentralized oracle network introduced Chainlink 24/7 on its X account, a market data service that extends pricing coverage for traditional financial assets to weekends and public holidays.

The service builds on Chainlink's existing 24/5 infrastructure, which provides pricing for more than $1.6 billion in tokenized equities across six blockchains and supports platforms including Ondo, xStocks, Robinhood, and Coinbase.

Previously, blockchain-based financial applications struggled to value traditional assets when their underlying markets closed, limiting trading opportunities and complicating collateral management.

Chainlink's new service addresses that gap by combining traditional market data during active trading sessions with perpetual-futures-derived pricing when exchanges are closed.

The infrastructure could support continuous trading in tokenized assets, derivatives, and prediction markets, while letting decentralized lending protocols manage collateral risks outside conventional market hours.

Aave, which had more than $34 billion in total value locked at the service's launch, is adopting the infrastructure through Horizon, its institutional lending platform, initially targeting tokenized US equities.

The expansion also affects LINK's economics.

Fidelity's ETF prospectus identifies demand for Chainlink's services as a factor influencing LINK's value, noting that the network converts certain fees paid in fiat currencies and other digital assets into LINK through its Payment Abstraction mechanism.

While Fidelity's expansion creates another avenue for investment demand, Chainlink's ability to generate additional fee-paying activity from always-on financial markets could provide a separate source of demand for its token.

#5022. Ukraine passes crypto market law, with $332 million revenue target

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The framework sets an 18% income tax and 5% military levy on crypto profits.

Ukraine’s parliament approved legislation covering virtual-asset trading, taxation and oversight.

In a statement on Wednesday, the Verkhovna Rada's press service said the parliament adopted the bill in its second reading and in full on Nov. 25. The legislation still requires the president’s signature and is scheduled to take effect July 1, 2027.

The framework ends a period of legal ambiguity that has engulfed the domestic crypto industry since 2022, when President Volodymyr Zelensky signed an earlier virtual assets law. That legislation never took effect because it required corresponding tax code changes.

Yaroslav Zhelezniak, a member of parliament in the Finance Committee, said in a Facebook post that the legislation represents "what was not possible for 35 years." He added that it could bring an additional 15 billion UAH ($332 million) in budget revenue.

The law sets requirements for companies operating with virtual assets and divides regulatory responsibilities between the National Securities and Stock Market Commission and the National Bank of Ukraine, according to the statement.

It also establishes investor-protection requirements, including greater transparency for market participants and the separation of client assets from companies’ own assets.

"The main goal of the adopted Law is not to restrain the development of new technologies, but to create conditions under which innovations will work transparently, responsibly, and in the interests of people, as well as taking into account the requirements for financial stability and security of the state," the press service wrote.

Zhelezniak said a preferential regime would impose a 5% income tax and 5% military levy through 2028. After that, the rates would rise to 18% and 5%, respectively.

The legislation follows three years of work on the framework, according to Zhelezniak.

#5020. NovaTech founders ordered to pay $1.3 billion over crypto Ponzi scheme targeting Haitian investors

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

In a statement on Wednesday, Attorney General Letitia James called the judgment historic and said it "delivers some semblance of justice."

Crypto trading platform NovaTech founders Cynthia and Eddy Petion have been ordered to pay over $1.3 billion after the state of New York sued the pair for defrauding investors in a Ponzi scheme targeting Haitian communities.

In a statement on Wednesday, New York Attorney General Letitia James called the judgment historic and said it "delivers some semblance of justice."

“NovaTech cruelly targeted immigrant families through faith and community groups with the promise of a better life while robbing them of their life savings," James added.

In 2024, James sued the married couple and others for defrauding thousands of investors, including at least 11,000 New Yorkers. Two companies were involved — crypto mining firm AWS Mining and NovaTech, which James said were pyramid schemes. AWS Mining promised investors a 200% guaranteed return, but collapsed in April 2019.

NovaTech then followed, which claimed to be a crypto and foreign exchange trading platform. Investors deposited over $1 billion worth of crypto into that later firm, but less than $26 million was ever traded on the platform, according to the complaint, which James called a Ponzi scheme because investors were promised profits but were paid from the crypto assets of other investors, not through trading.

Cynthia and Eddy Petion also specifically targeted investors of Haitian descent and the Haitian community in their ploys by promoting their schemes to investors in the Creole language and preying on their victims' religious faith, claiming they were marketed to those "most in need of income" and advertised the schemes as a means of “financial freedom," the NY Attorney General's office said.

The whereabouts of both Cynthia and Eddy Petion are unknown. In the previous complaint, the New York Attorney General's office said they secretly sold their house in Florida and fled to Panama in June 2022, allegedly transferring millions of dollars worth of crypto out of NovaTech, which then collapsed afterwards in 2023. They did not respond to or oppose NYAG's earlier complaint, the Supreme Court of the State of New York said in a court filing on Tuesday.

Correction: This story has been updated to reflect the $1.6 billion figure.

#5018. Bitcoin Has Become Boring, Finally

Bitcoin isn't a shiny new technology any more, it is established, and it is here to stay.

The 2019 Lightning conference in Berlin was lit: five hundred “cypherpunks” getting each other high on visions of a future with peer-to-peer electronic cash. Attending a bitcoin conference back in the day felt like being a teenager at a friend’s party while their parents were out of town. It was exciting and new. The feeling was the opposite of FOMO: something big was happening, we were on the inside, and the rest of the world was going to envy us. It was the kind of party that you could only have when the adults weren’t looking. Whenever someone bought a beer (with bitcoin), everyone would hoot and holler and record it on their phones for Instagram/Twitter (it was still called Twitter).

Lightning was the bleeding edge. We called it “the Lightning Network” (capitalized, if you please), and talking about it felt like talking about string theory: something so far out you’re not even sure it’s real. I spent a lot of time invoking the abacus.

Those are the times some of us remember fondly and keep trying to relive at bitcoin conferences today. That’s why we engage in rituals like drone shows, Satoshi Rockamoto sets, beefsteak dinners, and video game tournaments for sats, but it’s not the same. The ratio of bitcoin OG speakers to suits is shifting. Many event rooms are half empty, and the halls and meeting rooms are full of people negotiating cap tables and profit-sharing splits.

The adults haven’t shut the party down, but they have crashed it, and it kinda feels like their party now. The most exciting thing I noticed at the last bitcoin conference I attended was that nothing exciting happened.

The road to boring is seldom smooth. Technological innovation benefits from passion and bold ideas. People work harder on a project when they feel strongly about it and identify closely with like-minded collaborators. That’s where tech subcultures, their rituals, and their dogmas come from. But such passion and tribalism feed conflict, at least for a while until the tech goes mainstream, and normies, who couldn’t care less about subculture squabbles, take over.

This progression from an exciting new technology that inspires strong emotions to a humdrum utility is not unusual. World-changing innovations often (always?) start with a committed subculture that identifies fiercely with their weird tech before the mainstream adopts it and soon expects it. In fact, this trajectory has become the standard doctrine of tech marketing. For example, in the early days of the internet, early adopters wrote a Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace, picking a fight with states and corporations despite having nothing to back it up but chatrooms and dreams.

One case that resembles the early days of bitcoin was the war of the currents between high-voltage AC current and low-voltage DC current in the 1880s-1890s. Both featured big personalities stunning audiences with flashy demos at conferences. Edison and Westinghouse wowed crowds with their lightbulbs that made artificial light, just like bitcoiners in 2019 wowed YouTube by buying beer with bitcoin. And both cases featured rabid subcultures that accused each other of putting the future of the technology, if not of humanity, at stake. In the 1880s, the issue was whether AC was more deadly to humans and animals than DC; in the 2010s it was whether limiting the size of bitcoin’s blocks to 1MB would perpetuate monetary servitude forever.

In both cases, there were devoted subcultures whose disagreements helped the technology to mature before the tech crossed the chasm of exoticism to become the new, boring normal. Both are now largely managed by experts on pragmatic principles, not passionate conviction. Conferences went from spectacular showcases for technological miracles to sedate affairs where professionals debate and agree on industry standards. Pragmatism and consensus replaced ideology and dissent. In both instances things got boring, and boring was actually better.

Bitcoin is getting boring, although what that means and how it’s come to be that way depends on your point of view. As always, where you stand depends on where you sit.

Generally speaking, there are two broad points of view on what bitcoin is and is for. And though they started in different places, they’re both coming to a common conclusion: bitcoin is more boring than ever. So let’s review these two points of view, how they view bitcoin now, and why both would agree that the status quo is now so awfully, wonderfully boring.

The basic existential question that defined bitcoin’s first decade is settled: bitcoin is not a scam, and it’s not going away. That status is stable largely because bitcoin is now too big to fail, with a market cap exceeding a trillion dollars.

Much of this scale is thanks to the millions of people who want to own bitcoin as part of their savings, but not necessarily to trade and circulate it. In other words, they see bitcoin as a better form of gold, not cash. These savers want to integrate bitcoin into their fiat portfolio, just like any other asset. They aren’t terribly concerned about bitcoin’s status as a medium of exchange so long as it becomes firmly established as a viable, tradable commodity.

People investing in bitcoin are happy when the number goes up, and it generally does (you might have to zoom out on the price graph a bit, depending on the week). Bitcoin used to be a rollercoaster; now it’s more of a hike. The ups and downs still happen, but they’re gentler and a bit more predictable. How boring.

Bitcoin’s price started to settle down as mainstream finance started growing more comfortable with it as an asset. Whereas conventional finance used to want governments to shut bitcoin down, there is now about $100B worth of bitcoin held in ETFs and traded on ordinary equity markets. Major banks used to shun bitcoin, and now they accept it as collateral. Bitcoin is a regular feature in corporate treasuries, and some companies exist just to hold bitcoin. Strategy is worth about $55B on the open market, and it holds about $63B worth of bitcoin, so the entire company is a discounted bitcoin wallet. Bitcoin is also a regular feature in retirement accounts, pension allocations, and sovereign wealth funds. Thinking of bitcoin as another kind of asset ripe for institutional and retail investors now makes a lot of sense, because that’s what it is.

Why are these canny investors bored? It seems that all the exciting developments leading to bitcoin becoming a valuable asset have already happened. If the goal was integration into the world of conventional finance, it has incontrovertibly been achieved. You can’t YOLO on bitcoin any more than you can YOLO on gold. The milestones are all in the history section of the Wikipedia page, not on the roadmap.

People who wanted bitcoin to become a tradable asset are bored because mainstream finance has effectively tamed bitcoin. It is easily tradable, and its trading volumes are remarkable. It is digital gold, just with a slightly steeper curve and a little more volatility, which is exactly what these folks always wanted.

The main alternative to seeing bitcoin as a mainstream investment asset is to view it as monetary dynamite to ignite a revolution. People subscribing to this point of view wanted bitcoin to blossom into a system of peer-to-peer electronic cash that would first operate in parallel to the mainstream monetary system before supplanting it. These radicals wanted to see the banks collapse, not accept bitcoin as collateral. It was monetary insurrection, not incremental change.

This radical point of view is still around, but the wind has gone out of its combative sails for a few reasons.

First, there has been a generational shift. Many of the people who were pushing the revolutionary vision of bitcoin in their 20s fifteen years ago have moved on. Some got rich and retired or started to see and use bitcoin more as a tradable asset. For others, bitcoin never achieved the success they dreamt of, but it was successful enough that fighting for its future no longer felt necessary.

Second, AI is the new cool kid on the tech block. Instead of building vending machines for beer that accept bitcoin, enthusiasts who want to hack the system are now decompiling games with AI. No VC will waste a second on a pitch deck that doesn’t have AI on at least half of the slides. Miners are turning their server stacks and power contracts into AI data centers. Curious engineers have a new, much bigger toy to play with.

Third, mainstream bitcoin fans on Wall Street simply consume too much bandwidth. Not surprisingly, banks, publicly traded companies, and financial institutions with billions in their pockets are dominating panels at conferences and supplying the talking heads for financial news shows. They want to discuss topics like volatility and discount rates instead of personal sovereignty and individual financial freedom. Fighting against the system is not a narrative they can sell while representing the interests of that very system.

Fourth, bitcoin usage has moved past the radical mantras and progressed in a different direction. The dream of bitcoin becoming the standard payment medium in a circular economy where everyone buys coffee with bitcoin (why is it always coffee?) is starting to feel like an alternative history in a parallel universe.

A circular economy is simply not the role in society bitcoin has grown into. Instead of everyday payments, bitcoin is the medium of global value transfer. It has evolved into a technology to move real money across borders as remittances, into a settlement layer between various crypto assets, and into a store of value that people constantly buy, sell, and trade. It’s become a valuable network of rails that even stablecoins are happy to use.

Fixating on coffee purchases obscures the remarkable scale bitcoin has achieved. Somewhere between $1.6 and $4.1 trillion was settled on-chain between Q1 and Q3 2026 (depending on how you count). PayPal processed $1.79 trillion in all of 2025. The average payment on PayPal is about $70. The average bitcoin transaction (using the strict counting method) is $10,000. With bitcoin moving trillions in value, we can stop worrying about coffee.

Bitcoin may not have cornered retail payments, but it’s a mature and highly liquid asset. It’s an industry unto itself. It has found its place in the economy, and it’s thriving. Despite the lack of revolutionary fireworks, bitcoin is changing mainstream finance by opening new possibilities and financially enfranchising new user groups. That’s still worth celebrating.

You know what’s really boring? Electricity infrastructure. You know what no one can live without despite how boring it is? Electricity infrastructure.

When revolutionary technologies fade into the background of everyday life, when people use them constantly without thinking about them, they become boring, and they become essential. Buying a beer with Lightning is no longer exciting because we can now expect that it will just work without fanfare. Being able to say “it will just work” sounds boring, but it’s a clear sign of triumph.

Bitcoiners and builders need to adjust to this beautiful, boring reality. We can stop annoying our neighbors with orange pills. It’s about utility, not evangelism. Utility means building rails that bitcoin and stablecoins can use together seamlessly, adding bitcoin to mainstream fintech apps, and building new financial applications on top of the bitcoin chain. Perhaps none of this will light the fireworks at the radicals’ victory party or replace T-bills as the base layer of global finance, but every user who discovers the unique utility of bitcoin is further evidence of its mainstream adoption.

What we have is a thriving technology that enables us to do miraculous new things, and it’s achieved an undeniable scale, such that it is now too big to fail. That’s fantastic. It may not be the future we were dreaming about seven years ago in Berlin, but it’s wonderful in its own right, and it’s worth cultivating and celebrating.

Even though nobody sets out to grow up and become boring one day, it’s still a valid kind of success. It means you’ve made it, and you’re doing fine. Boring is what happens when things just work and things have just worked out. So we didn’t break the world with bitcoin. Oh well. We’re making a new one. A party with adults present is still a party. And maybe we’re now the adults. So dance while you wait for the dollar to collapse 😉

#5017. Tesla on Autopilot/FSD hit an overturned truck at 71 mph, killing 3

A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, at 71 mph.

Police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data, and it lands as Tesla’s monthly crash count hits another record.

Just before 4 a.m. on Sunday, May 31, 2026, the 31-year-old driver of a 2014 Freightliner lost the road near the Pine Ridge Road exit in Collier County, steered back onto southbound I-75, and flipped it, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The overturned truck ended up blocking the center and outside lanes.

Jonathan Garcia Arias, a 25-year-old Naples man and former Marine, was driving by in a BMW. He pulled over and got out to help the truck driver.

Then a southbound 2023 Tesla with five young men from Naples inside came up on the scene. FHP’s report says the front of the Tesla hit the underside of the overturned truck and Garcia Arias. Two of the Tesla’s passengers, aged 18 and 19, died at the scene, and Garcia Arias died later in the hospital. The 20-year-old driver and two more passengers were seriously hurt.

A few days later, FHP used the crash as a warning about stopping near wrecks on the interstate. Senior Trooper Kenn Watson said the Tesla driver would have seen only the truck’s underside, with “no lights, no reflectors, nothing warning them.”

So that’s the official story. A dark obstacle, a driver who couldn’t see it in time. Nobody said a word about Autopilot.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone was killed or hurt. Tesla filed one for this crash.

It identifies the car as a 2023 Model 3 on a highway, flags a traffic incident on the roadway, and marks the automation “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That means Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 71 mph and a fatality, lists the Florida Highway Patrol as the investigating agency, and says it learned of the crash from police and the media.

Then it blacks out the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating domain, all as “confidential business information.” That’s the same redaction Tesla applies to 99.9% of its reports.

The report also surfaced late. Tesla filed it as a 5-Day report, the urgent category for fatal crashes, but it didn’t land until Tesla’s September filings, more than three months after the crash. And Tesla lists law enforcement as one of the ways it found out about it.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 07:56 UTC, which converts to 3:56 a.m. in Florida, two minutes off the 3:54 a.m. in FHP’s report. The city, the highway, the 2023 model year, the month and the fatal outcome all line up, and it’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report in Naples that month. It’s the same crash.

A Tesla on driver-assist going highway speed into the underside of a big truck, in the dark, in Florida. If that sounds familiar, it should.

In 2016, Joshua Brown was killed near Williston when his Model S on Autopilot drove under a tractor-trailer crossing the highway. In 2019, Jeremy Banner died in Delray Beach when his Model 3 on Autopilot went under a trailer at 68 mph and had its roof sheared off. In both crashes, neither the driver nor the system braked.

Trooper Watson’s point was that a human couldn’t see the truck. But a big, unlit obstacle sitting across two lanes at night is exactly the kind of thing a driver-assist system is supposed to catch, and Tesla now sells FSD as nearly ready to drive with nobody watching. And an attentive driver could clearly see it, as the BMW driver did, and stop before the Tesla arrived.

We want to be fair about what the data doesn’t prove. “Engaged within 30 seconds” is the reporting trigger. Tesla’s 71 mph may be a telematics snapshot rather than the impact speed. And with the software version redacted, we can’t say whether this was Autopilot or FSD.

The NHTSA release that surfaced this crash, covering filings through October 15, also set a new monthly high. Tesla reported 264 driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236, which was itself a record. That’s up from 135 in March.

September may still grow as late reports come in. This Naples crash shows how late they can be.

Our merged dataset now holds 4,669 Tesla driver-assist crash reports since 2019, 69 of them flagged fatal. The same release added two other fatal reports, both “Verified Engaged” and both covered locally with no mention of driver-assist: a Model Y that hit a tree and burned in El Dorado Hills, California, killing three, and a Model X that hit a signal pole in Naples on September 30, killing a passenger. We’ll lay those out separately.

Three people died on I-75, including a man who got out of his car to help a stranger. Tesla knows its driver-assist was on, knows the speed, holds the telematics, and filed a federal report saying so. Then it sealed everything that would explain what the car did, and the public got a story about a dark truck.

That's what happens when the system has to identify all objects in the camera frame before it can start to estimate the objects position and then relative distance and then relative velocity. Unrecognizable objects will destroy all your logic. This is a design failure and not something Tesla can actually fix.

Compare that to radars and lidars that directly measure distances and relative velocities of everything in front of the car, regardless of what it is. That is a far better approach because you do not want the car the impact objects on its trajectory regardless of what those objects turn out to be.

Tesla’s whole pitch for FSD is that the car sees better than you do, and yet, Tesla vehicles on Autopilot and FSD keep crashing on stationary objects on the highway. It’s the same failure that killed Joshua Brown and Jeremy Banner years ago. If the system saw the truck and the driver overrode it, Tesla should say so. It was quick to do that in the Katy crash when the data helped it. If the system didn’t see it, that’s a safety defect regulators and owners need to know about.

Either way, the redaction protects Tesla, not the people on the road. It’s the same pattern we found in Vineland and in July’s four fatal crashes, and the crash count keeps setting records.

We’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol for the full crash report, whether its investigators got Tesla’s raw vehicle data, and whether they even knew the system was engaged. If they didn’t, the only party that knows what this car did is the one that sealed the file.

#5015. Wall Street and Crypto Are in 'Extreme Fear'. What's Spooking Investors?

Wall Street and Crypto Are in 'Extreme Fear'. What's Spooking Investors?

Investors in both the stock and cryptocurrency markets are back in panic mode Tuesday, just one day after Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO triggered a massive rally across risk assets.

Bitcoin is trading at around $59,500, down 2.74% since the daily session opened, while the total cryptocurrency market capitalization has fallen 4.44% to $2.04 trillion, per CoinMarketCap. The Nasdaq and S&P 500 are also in the red, giving back some of Monday's gains.

CoinMarketCap's Fear and Greed Index (which tracks the sentiment across all the crypto market) currently sits at 9 out of 100, matching Friday's reading, the lowest since February. Just three months ago, the same indicator reached its yearly high of 82, corresponding to extreme greed.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Over on Wall Street, CNN's equivalent sits at 17, also in extreme fear territory, after reaching its lowest level since March on Friday.

Both indexes measure investor sentiment on a scale from zero to 100, with lower readings indicating greater fear. They use different methodologies, incorporating market momentum, volatility, and trading behavior rather than simply asking investors how they feel.

The artificial intelligence industry, largely responsible for Wall Street's extraordinary performance over the past few years, is now at the center of the selloff.

Last week, the Nasdaq lost approximately 10%, its worst weekly performance since 2020, wiping out its gains for the year. The S&P 500 entered correction territory, having fallen more than 10% from its October peak.

Nvidia's leadership crisis made things considerably worse. The world's leading AI chipmaker had lost nearly half its market value from its October highs before the company's board reinstated Jensen Huang on Monday, sending its shares up 31.5% by the closing bell.

But having Huang back at Nvidia doesn't necessarily make AI investments more profitable.

Investors are increasingly questioning whether the hundreds of billions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure will generate enough revenue to justify the expense. As Decrypt previously reported, 52% of respondents to Bank of America's November fund manager survey expect at least one major cloud computing company to announce spending cuts within six months.

Anthropic's much-anticipated IPO hasn't helped much, either. Shares of the Claude developer fell below their $83 offering price Tuesday, less than a week after the company made its stock market debut at $111.50.

Nvidia fell 5.8% during early trading Tuesday, while AI infrastructure providers CoreWeave and IREN lost 6.9% and 9%, respectively. Healthcare and consumer staples stocks were doing considerably better, suggesting investors are moving money into businesses less dependent on the AI boom.

An additional concern for both markets is that the U.S. Federal Reserve could make money more expensive at precisely the moment the AI industry needs more of it.

Traders are pricing in a 98% probability of a December interest rate hike and a 66% chance of another increase in January, according to CME FedWatch data.

Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for companies building data centers and reduce the present value of their expected future profits. They also make government bonds more attractive relative to speculative assets such as Bitcoin, which doesn't generate income for its holders.

For crypto investors, this comes at a particularly bad time.

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded another $569.7 million in net withdrawals on Monday, despite Bitcoin's brief recovery, per Decrypt’s ETF tracker. BlackRock's IBIT alone accounted for $509.3 million.

November's cumulative Bitcoin ETF outflows have now reached $4.71 billion, surpassing June's previous monthly record with four trading sessions still remaining.

Bitcoin's daily chart shows a cryptocurrency struggling to hold a price range that has served as support on several occasions since 2024.

BTC has lost approximately 53% of its value from its October 2025 all-time high, and the recovery that took Bitcoin above $85,000 in September has largely evaporated.

The $60,000 area is particularly relevant because buyers stepped in around similar prices in February and June. Friday's dip toward $55,000 established another potential support area, with historical buying activity around $50,000 further below.

Extreme fear readings have historically coincided with some attractive buying opportunities, but they are notoriously unreliable at identifying the exact bottom. Bitcoin can remain oversold for extended periods, particularly when institutional investors are pulling billions of dollars out of the market.

Investors will get another important piece of economic data Wednesday, when the U.S. releases its Personal Consumption Expenditures inflation report, the Fed's preferred measure of inflation and the last major data release before its December monetary policy meeting.

#5014. Aave Labs publicly launches savings app as balances top $63 million

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The Aave App offers a variable 6% base rate for 90 days on balances of up to $100,000 for verified users.

Aave Labs launched its Aave App to the public on Wednesday following an early access phase that attracted more than $63 million in user balances in under three months.

The savings app seeks to combine the simplicity of modern fintech apps with the earning opportunities and efficiency of onchain finance, alongside bank connectivity in the U.S., UK, and the EEA, with no fees on bank deposits and withdrawals, Aave Labs said in a statement shared with The Block. Users can open self-custodial Aave Accounts with an email address or phone number and a password, without manually setting up a conventional crypto wallet, storing a recovery phrase, or paying blockchain transaction fees themselves, the firm added.

The app is available on iOS and Android. Early access began on iOS on Aug. 26, with Android early access following on Nov. 17 after the app attracted a waitlist of "tens of thousands of people," according to Aave Labs.

"Aave App makes the benefits of onchain finance accessible to everyday users, creating a better way to save," Aave Labs founder and CEO Stani Kulechov said. "The industry is at an important moment. The technologies that power onchain finance have finally come together in a way that allows the complexity to fade into the background."

Plans for the app were initially unveiled last November. At the time, Aave advertised rates of up to 9% and "insurance-backed protection" on deposits of up to $1 million. Aave Labs sought $5 million from the Aave DAO for the Aave App in February.

At public launch, Aave App offers verified users a variable 6% base rate for 90 days on balances of up to $100,000, Aave Labs said, adding that eligible users can lift that to 7.25% through referrals and recurring deposits. Users can withdraw without a penalty, while earnings accrue from the time of deposit and compound every second, according to the firm, though it noted that eligibility and availability vary by market.

Eligible users in the U.S., excluding New York, can move money between their bank accounts and Aave App through licensed third-party providers, including Bridge and Astra. Push by Aave Labs provides the same connection in the UK and EEA, according to the statement. Users in other supported jurisdictions can deposit USDC, USDT, or GHO stablecoins from eight networks: Ethereum, Arbitrum, Base, BNB Chain, HyperEVM, Monad, Optimism, and TRON. Aave Labs said it will continue to expand bank connectivity as licensing and banking partnerships allow.

Deposits are supplied to lending markets on the Aave Protocol, the largest onchain lending protocol by total value locked, where borrower interest payments generate earnings for savers. The Aave Protocol uses an overcollateralized lending model, meaning borrowers deposit assets worth more than they borrow. Aave App’s Stable Vaults allocate funds among supported markets under preset rules, meaning users see a single savings balance without needing to manage stablecoins, networks, or lending markets themselves.

The app's discretionary Balance Protection program may reimburse eligible users for certain losses tied to security incidents, technology failures, and extended account lockouts, subject to its terms, Aave Labs said. Lockton placed supporting insurance arrangements with Relm Insurance, with part of the risk reinsured by Munich Re, but users do not hold insurance under the program. However, funds in Aave App are not bank deposits or covered by FDIC or SIPC insurance.

Aave Labs said it expects to expand the platform with additional financial products and capabilities over time.

#5012. Tesla on Autopilot/FSD was going 74 mph before fiery crash that killed 3

A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, with the car doing 74 mph.

The crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck. None of that coverage mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

Late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway. That’s a residential part of the Serrano community in El Dorado Hills, east of Sacramento.

According to the CHP’s Placerville office, the Model Y left the road “for unknown reasons,” hit a tree on the north side of the parkway, and caught fire. Officers got the call around 10:38 p.m. By the time they arrived, the car was fully engulfed in flames.

Charles Anthony Cameron, 30, of Sacramento, was thrown from the car and died at the scene. Alejandra Mendoza, 28, of Sacramento, and Kailauna Viola Mills, 28, of Roseville, were found dead inside once firefighters put out the fire. One of the two women was driving; CHP hasn’t publicly said which.

Mills lived in Arizona and was visiting family. Her uncle told CBS Sacramento she worked in the medical field and was supposed to get married next April.

A fourth person, a 28-year-old Sacramento woman, survived with major injuries.

CHP says the cause is still under investigation. Speed, impairment, and how the car left the road haven’t been released. And nobody has said a word about Autopilot.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

It lists a 2024 Model Y, a consumer vehicle, and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That’s Tesla confirming through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 74 mph, a fatality, and the California Highway Patrol as the investigating agency.

Then it redacts the narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

The rest of the report is strangely thin. Tesla lists the roadway type as “Unknown” and what the car hit as “Unknown,” even though police said it was a tree. It checks only one source for how it learned of the crash: the media. So Tesla found out about a triple-fatal crash in one of its cars from the news, then went into its own data and confirmed its driver-assist was on.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 05:36 UTC, which is 10:36 p.m. Pacific on September 12, within two minutes of the 10:38 p.m. call CHP responded to. The city, the 2024 Model Y, the month, and the fatal outcome all line up. It’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report from El Dorado Hills in the data. It’s the same crash.

Two of the three victims were found inside the car after the fire was out. The survivor got out of, or was pulled from, the wreckage, depending on the report.

CHP hasn’t said whether the doors played any role, and we’re not suggesting they did. But it’s a fair question to ask about any Tesla crash with a fire, now that NHTSA is writing new rules for emergency door releases after years of complaints about people getting trapped. We’ve asked.

This is the second triple-fatal crash in Tesla’s latest NHTSA filings where its driver-assist was verified engaged and the public never heard about it. The other one was on I-75 in Naples. Add Vineland and July’s four fatal crashes, and the pattern is hard to miss.

"what little effort went into the report"?

I disagree, a lot of effort went in to minimize the report, to portray it as an unremarkable accident.

That is the effort I find Tesla criminally responsible for.

The CHP need the full report, no redactions. If they chose to censor it that is their task, not Tesla's.

What stands out in this one is how little effort went into the report. Tesla knows the speed, knows the system was on, and has telematics. But it couldn’t fill in what the car hit, and it learned about three deaths in one of its cars from the news. Then it redacted the one field, the narrative, that would tell us what the car did.

Tesla wants regulators and customers to trust FSD with no one watching. That trust has to be earned with data. A company that seals the account of what its car did at 74 mph in a neighborhood, in a crash that killed three people, isn’t earning it.

We’re asking CHP Placerville whether its investigators knew the system was engaged, whether they got Tesla’s raw data or Tesla’s summary of it, and what they found about the fire and the doors. If CHP never got the full data, how will it ever determine the cause?

#5008. South Korea Moves to Lift Its ICO Ban After Nearly a Decade

South Korea Moves to Lift Its ICO Ban After Nearly a Decade

South Korea is proposing to end its nine-year ban on initial coin offerings, a move aimed at pulling crypto fundraising back onshore, creating jobs and folding token sales into a regulated framework.

The country’s Financial Services Commission unveiled a draft bill, the Act on Digital Asset Industry Innovation and User Protection, on Tuesday that would reverse the prohibition imposed in September 2017, when regulators banned ICOs over fraud, speculation and investor losses.

If passed, it would let domestic projects issue and sell tokens to the public for the first time in nearly a decade.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Under the proposal, any issuer would have to file a “digital asset white paper” with the FSC before selling tokens, detailing the project, how the raised funds will be used, how many tokens will be issued and the risks involved. Issuers and their executives would face civil damages, financial penalties and possible criminal prosecution for false or omitted information, a liability regime modeled on the disclosure rules governing stock offerings.

The ban, regulators have concluded, never really worked. It largely pushed Korean projects to set up entities abroad and run their token sales through them, with game developers Wemade and Netmarble among the better-known firms that took the offshore route. The FSC’s stated goal is to reclaim that activity and the investment and jobs that went with it.

The ICO reversal is one piece of a sweeping overhaul. The same bill would restrict issuance of Korean won-backed stablecoins to consortiums in which commercial banks hold a majority stake, cap any single major shareholder’s ownership of a crypto exchange at 20% (rising to 34% under certain conditions), extend market-manipulation rules to crypto-to-crypto trades, and organize the market into regulated verticals spanning exchanges, trading, brokerage, custody and asset management.

The shift fits a broader global move toward regulated token fundraising, as the U.S. and others build out frameworks that give crypto issuers clearer legal footing. It also marks a notable turn for South Korea, one of the world’s most active retail crypto markets, which has long paired enthusiastic trading with strict rules.

The proposal is only a draft. It now heads to the National Assembly, where lawmakers must approve it before any of the changes take effect, leaving the timeline, and the final shape of the rules, still to be determined.

Another bonus: There’s a smaller pocket tucked into the back with a single zipper, which makes it ideal for hiding cash, cards, and other small valuables.

Thanks to the water-resistant nylon exterior, anything stowed away will remain dry, in the event it starts pouring rain. Our favorite part, however, is the strap that we found to be one of the most comfortable ones that we’ve tested. As for the colorway, you can choose from a bunch of neutral tones, but our fashion team recommends going with the eucalyptus hue—you’re bound to be the center of attention.

While it can’t store a water bottle, we love how effortlessly our gadgets and snacks fit inside. Not to mention, it has so much versatility in regard to style. You can wear it with your best sweatsuit or casual fit and look fly for the day’s festivities.

This Amazon best-seller is spot-on for your next adventure. It’s really got organization in spades with mesh pockets on two sides for bottles or umbrellas, a small front zipper pocket for smaller devices, and a big space inside that’s designed like a backpack. It’s smartly compartmentalized into smaller sections for anything from keys, passports, snacks, and other bits and bobs. During a camping trip, we made use of the main pocket inside, which is big enough to store your phone and tablet, a feature that we deemed essential in a travel sling bag.

You can even enjoy your music on your commute as the convenient opening on the front provides easy access to your earphones. It comes in every color imaginable, but the teal blue and reflective details will help you stand out and offer nighttime visibility. And unlike others in this guide, this one comes with a water bottle holder, so you stay hydrated on the move.

As one of the smaller sling bags in our guide, the Topo Designs Mini Quick Pack has substantial storage where it matters most. We found that its capacity is perfect for shorter trips and daily errands, and the straps are a piece of cake to adjust (though there are quite a few straps). Whenever we don’t need a huge backpack and want to pack light, this little guy is a star.

In our experience, we’ve worn it on the waist and across the body. One tester was able to utilize the bike light attachment loop for a nighttime ride to increase visibility. And with a solid amount of space and interior organization for a phone, cardholder, and other odds and ends, our editors have also tucked it under a thin coat when we’re in a tight spot. Plus, the unique color-blocked design earns it some extra style points.

While we still feel it works great for the city, this ruggedly built sling is perfect for outdoor adventurists. Firstly, it’s offered in two different sizes with a 6- or 9-liter size, ensuring that if you need a little extra space, you can spend an extra $10 to upgrade. Even in the smaller size, you can easily fit a water bottle plus all of your other gear like earbuds, sunglasses, phone, EDC essentials, protein bar, plus more thanks to the expandable gusset.

One of the cool features of this bag that you won’t find on others is that it comes with sturdy quick-release buckles on both sides, making it ideal no matter which shoulder you toss it around. It offers various storage compartments, 10 to be exact, even with a soft-lined pouch that is great for your phone or sunglasses, helping to avoid scratching while on the move—plus, the padded back and bottom help to protect everything else. The shell’s made from abrasion-resistant polyester fabric, the same ultra-tough material as the brand’s duffels, which are designed for actual expeditions, so your daily commute? No sweat.

There’s a padded sleeve that snugly fits a tablet, reflective accents for low-light visibility (great for late-night rides), and a thick, padded shoulder strap that’s actually comfortable to wear all day. Eddie Bauer’s Mini Crossbody Bag proves that you don’t have to spend big to get a reliable everyday carry. Made from nylon, this compact bag punches above its weight when it comes to utility. During testing, we found the slightly 0.8L capacity to be just right. It’s big enough to fit your phone, wallet, keys, and a lip balm, but small enough to stay light and nimble when you’re clocking your daily step count goal. I love the front cargo pocket that has a flap closure. It kept essentials like subway cards or AirPods secure but easy to access when we were on the go.

Yeah, it’s too small to carry a tablet or water bottle, but it comes in clutch for light carry days and quick errands. One tester wore it on a weekend trip and appreciated how easy it was to sling over a jacket without ever feeling bulky. The strap adjusts smoothly and stays comfortable during hours of walking, and after a few days of use, the bag still looked good as new.

Reigning Champ’s crossbody bag is reliable for outdoor gear because it combines smart construction and water-resistant materials. This resilient twill bag is the practical choice to go anywhere, and though it may look compact, there’s plenty of space and interior pockets to keep your stuff organized without looking overloaded. I even wore this during a rainy evening commute, and everything inside, from my phone to loose bills, stayed bone dry.

With it, you get two main zippered pockets, plus an internal zippered pocket, and you even get a small front-facing zippered pocket for quick access when you need it. Another thing that we really like about this bag is the ability to loosen (or tighten) the quick-adjuster and padded straps while still wearing it.

While this bag is designed with creatives in mind to be able to hold all of your tech, like cameras, laptops (depending on size choice), lenses, rangefinders, and more (thanks to its comfy and padded design), it can still be a great option to use hiking or biking with its weatherproof design and 400D shell construction. While it is resistant to the elements, some reviewers do mention to be cautious with heavier rainfall, though the majority note it can handle most situations.

Traveling around the city, either to and from work, running errands, or just heading to the local coffee shop means finding a bag that’s just big enough to hold the essentials, yet one that’s not gonna weigh you down. Aer’s City Sling 2 is the perfectly sized bag for city activities and commuting. It weighs under a pound and holds 2.5 liters, which means you can still get all of your EDC gear in there with ease.

Even though it’s lightweight, it’s darn tough with its 700D Cordura nylon design and aircraft-grade aluminum tension locks, which means you don’t sacrifice durability. It has a quick-access front pocket for things like keychains, while its back zippered pocket is better for valuables like passports or wallets, with ample room in its main zippered compartment, too. Plus, its strap hides away thanks to its magnetic fastener, converting it into a mobile dopp kit in a pinch. While the strap is tough, it may be a little rough on the shoulder after a day of wear.

Oakley’s Extractor Sling is basically a backpack in disguise, making it perfect for work commutes. It has the capacity to serve as one with several compartments and pockets to transport goods like your hand cream, portable charger, and office laptop. We found this sling bag specifically useful for when we want to pack more without overdoing it.

You can even fit your gym shorts and workout shirts inside to hit a quick session once you’re off the clock. Plus, the back panel is equipped with air channels to help deliver more breathability and comfort while you’re on the move. Although the downside is that it is heavier than others we’ve tested, it’s got the volume you need to load it all in.

The best sling bags for men should offer features that cater to your needs. Typically smaller than a messenger bag, they can be worn across the body, over a shoulder, or even around the waist. The sling bags in our guide range from 1.5 liters of capacity to 30 liters.

When looking for one, consider the layout and accessibility of the compartments, pockets, and dedicated spaces for laptops, smartphones, tablets, or water bottles. All in all, there should be ample storage capacity (usually measured and listed in liters) that allows for smart organization and easy reach.

Since sling bags are often worn over one shoulder or across the body, the best sling bags for men need to have adjustable straps and padding to distribute weight evenly across your shoulders and back—a properly fitted sling bag should feel comfortable and not strain you even when worn for extended periods. Therefore, pay attention to the strap’s material, width, and adjustability.

A lightweight sling bag is usually better since it is easier to carry and feels better on your body by preventing unnecessary strain on your shoulders and back, especially if you plan to use the sling bag for hours on end, or carry it while hiking. Ultimately, the weight of a sling bag will depend on the bag's capacity, design, and intended uses.

To find the best sling bags for men, myself and Joseph Cheatham, led by our Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower, put them through real-life situations. We loaded them up with our usual gear like our phone, wallet, keys, snacks, even a water bottle to see how they handle the weight. The ones we tested have been worn at outdoor festivals, during day hikes, through long-haul flights, and of course, out and about running weekend errands. We paid close attention to the pockets and zippers, but really made sure to assess how comfortable the adjustable straps lie on our shoulders.

Many sling bags are actually designed to accommodate laptops or tablets. These sling bags usually fall on the larger, more functional side, with a large capacity and spacious interior compartment, as well as dedicated padded compartments or sleeves that offer protection and secure storage for your electronic devices.

Sling bags are versatile just like backpacks, hence, with the right style and design, they can work in a variety of places. A sleek, leather option looks professional enough for the office and goes well with your office fits. A rugged, weather-resistant one is great for outdoor activities—in fact, there are sling bags designed for purposes like hiking and traveling. For your casual outings, a small, stylish sling bag will work wonders.

The settlement was filed Nov. 24 in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, bringing a seven-year legal battle closer to a conclusion.

Nvidia has agreed to pay $290 million to settle a long-running securities class-action lawsuit alleging it misled investors about the extent of cryptocurrency mining demand contributing to its gaming GPU sales in 2017 and 2018.

The proposed settlement, which still requires court approval, resolves claims that Nvidia and CEO Jensen Huang understated crypto miners' contributions to gaming revenue and failed to disclose the risks posed by a subsequent collapse in mining demand, driven largely by a slump in Ethereum mining. Plaintiffs alleged that the disclosures contributed to a 28.5% drop in Nvidia's stock over two trading sessions in November 2018.

Nvidia said its insurers are funding the majority of the $290 million settlement, while plaintiffs' attorneys are requesting up to $62 million in legal fees from the fund.

The settlement was filed Nov. 24 in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, bringing a seven-year legal battle closer to a conclusion.

The case was dismissed in 2021 but revived by the Ninth Circuit in 2023, and a federal judge certified it as a class action earlier this year.

In a separate case, Nvidia settled with the Securities and Exchange Commission for $5.5 million over similar disclosures concerning the impact of crypto mining on its gaming business.

The settlement comes amid a volatile month for Nvidia, the world's most valuable company.

Nvidia's stock (NVDA) has swung sharply following reports earlier this month that cofounder and longtime CEO Jensen Huang had resigned amid allegations of multiple affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

The board subsequently voted to reinstate Huang on Monday, sending the stock surging more than 30% before renewed selling pressure hit the broader technology sector as concerns over AI valuations rattled markets.

#5004. What the CFTC’s New Crypto Reserves Guidance Actually Allows—And What It Doesn’t

What the CFTC’s New Crypto Reserves Guidance Actually Allows—And What It Doesn’t

The U.S. derivatives regulator has quietly opened the door for crypto exchanges and clearinghouses to hold Bitcoin, Ethereum, and stablecoins as part of the financial cushion they’re required to keep, the latest sign of the agency weaving digital assets into the plumbing of regulated markets.

But the fine print matters, and it draws a careful line.

In a staff advisory issued this week, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s Division of Market Oversight and Division of Clearing and Risk explained how swap execution facilities, designated contract markets, and derivatives clearing organizations can use crypto assets to meet their financial-resources requirements.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Those rules require such platforms to hold enough resources to cover at least 12 months of operating costs, a buffer meant to ensure a venue can keep running or wind down safely if it hits trouble.

Here’s what the guidance allows: Certain crypto assets, specifically naming Bitcoin, Ethereum, and payment stablecoins, can now count toward that 12-month requirement, subject to “appropriate haircuts,” meaning their value would be discounted to account for volatility. That’s a meaningful concession, effectively recognizing crypto as a legitimate corporate reserve asset for the firms the CFTC oversees.

Here’s what it doesn’t allow, and this is the catch that defines the policy: Crypto can’t be counted toward a separate liquidity requirement.

Because digital assets don’t qualify as “cash” or “highly liquid securities” under Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, they fall short of that stricter test. In practice, a platform can hold Bitcoin or Ethereum as part of its longer-term financial backstop, but it still needs traditional cash-like instruments on hand to satisfy the rule meant to ensure it can pay obligations quickly.

The distinction is the whole point. It lets firms treat crypto as a store of value on their balance sheets while reinforcing that, when it comes to assets that must be instantly spendable, volatile tokens still don’t make the cut.

The nuance is easy to miss, but it reflects a measured posture from a regulator that has otherwise moved aggressively on crypto.

The CFTC has already previously cleared perpetual futures on individual stocks, issued no-action relief letting crypto apps offer regulated derivatives, and floated a plan to bring crypto exchanges under federal oversight, part of a broader push to set digital-asset policy on its own authority.

That said, it’s worth noting that the advisory represents the views of CFTC staff only. It creates no new rules or enforceable rights, isn’t a no-action position, and doesn’t necessarily reflect the views of the Commission itself.

It could also shift as the agency’s makeup changes. President Donald Trump recently sent a bipartisan slate of nominees to fill vacant CFTC and SEC seats, which could reshape the commissions now steering crypto policy.

For now, the guidance is best read not as crypto winning blanket acceptance as a reserve asset, but as the CFTC sorting out precisely where digital assets fit, and where they still don’t, in the machinery of regulated trading.

On Tuesday, the DOJ said it targeted more than 800 defendants and helped law enforcement in almost a dozen countries in raids on scam call centers and compounds.

Following President Donald Trump's directive to crack down on fraud and predatory schemes, the Justice Department announced what it called its "largest-ever crackdown," targeting scammers in Southeast Asia and bad actors using digital assets to launder billions of dollars.

On Tuesday, the DOJ said it targeted more than 800 defendants and helped law enforcement in almost a dozen countries in raids on scam call centers and compounds.

"The unprecedented results of this surge are just the beginning," said Attorney General Todd Blanche in a statement. "We will continue prosecuting those who perpetrate these schemes and disrupting the activities of transnational criminal organizations before they reach American shores."

In March, Trump signed an executive order directing the Secretary of State, the Attorney General, and other officials to review their regulatory frameworks to figure out how best to combat crime, particularly related to cyber and predatory schemes against people in the U.S. Trump specifically directed Blanche to prioritize crime involving scam centers.

One of those cases was against Cambodia-based Huione Group, an organization that had been accused of laundering billions of dollars in crypto fraud proceeds. In June, the Justice Department said it had seized a cloud computing account, which it said had been used as "a technological backbone that allowed billions in fraud proceeds to be transferred, moved, and concealed," often through Southeast Asian scam centers.

The State Department also funded efforts by U.S. and Southeast Asian law enforcement to help freeze more than $1 billion in stolen crypto, the DOJ said Tuesday.

"State Department-funded forensic tools helped analyze more than 10,000 devices and hard drives in Thailand alone, allowing U.S. and Thai law enforcement to better understand the criminal networks and advance U.S. investigations," the DOJ said.

The State Department also targeted Moldova, where it trained local prosecutors and provided equipment that then helped with raids in October that ended in the closure of five call centers and five people arrested for allegedly running a fake crypto trading platform, according to the DOJ.

The crackdown comes as the Trump administration has pursued a largely pro-crypto agenda, pledging to make the U.S. the global capital of the digital asset industry and rolling back regulations it views as limiting innovation. But that approach has drawn criticism from lawmakers, particularly over Trump's personal and family-linked crypto ventures and potential conflicts of interest.

#5001. The 12 Best Swim Trunks for Men of 2026, Worn and Tested by Style Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Our editors recommend shorts from Rhone and Fair Harbor.

SUMMER MAY BE behind us, but that doesn’t mean your swim trunks need to go into hibernation. If you’re planning to escape the cold for somewhere sunny this winter, a good pair should be in your suitcase. The beauty of men’s swim trunks is that they can be worn in or out of the water, doubling as the ultimate beachside bottoms or everyday shorts. The best swim trunks for men today have a moisture-wicking and quick-drying fabric, four-way stretch for mobility, a flattering length, and an athletic fit. Finding the right one for you can be a challenge, which is why we're here to help. Our team of fashion editors spent the past year trying and testing swim trunks to find options that blend comfort and style.

Over the past four years, I’ve tested more than 20 different pairs of swim trunks—everything from legacy surf brands to buzzy newcomers—but Fair Harbor’s have consistently exceeded my expectations. This pair nails that trifecta of being stylish, functional, and worth the price.

The first thing I noticed: the fabric. It’s a cotton-poly blend that feels smooth and broken-in right out of the gate. It doesn’t feel like any of that stiff, swishy, overly synthetic feel you get with most swim trunks. I’m usually quick to write off built-in liners altogether, but the BreezeKnit liner changed my mind. It feels more like a supportive pair of boxer briefs than the usual scratchy mesh. It’s snug (but comfortable on the crown jewels), breathable, and, most importantly, it doesn’t ride up or chafe. I’ve worn it for full beach days in Puerto Rico—swimming, walking, grabbing lunch—and never once felt the need to adjust.

The 7-inch inseam hits just above the knee on me, giving it a clean, tailored look. It’s an easy middle ground that works whether you’re getting in the water or just wearing it as your default summer short. There’s enough stretch in the cotton-polyester fabric that I never feel restricted. Plus, it comes in seersucker versions, solid-colored options, and other unique patterns. The hidden zipper pocket stashes a key or card without them slipping out, and the side pockets don’t balloon up in the water—something a lot of trunks still get wrong. It’s not a substitute for a gym short, but the fabric dries quickly for other oceanside activities.

I can’t get enough of the R&R Trunk's timeless style, functional fabric, and flattering fit. I love the no-fuss design with a tailored cut that’s not too baggy or slim. Coupled with the flexible waistband, the fit looks great on most body types. It’s available in two inseams–5.5 and 7.5 inches. The latter provides enough coverage and hits a couple inches above the knee for most men (our universal style recommendation for shorts). Though I wore the shorter length on the beach during my stay in Miami because it shows off my summer leg gains.

Rhone’s athleisure performs just as well as it looks. I’ve sweat-tested the R&R during beachside runs and volleyball games, and found that its odor-fighting fabric kept me feeling fresh. The mesh liner kept my family jewels locked in, without cutting off circulation. A few editors on our style team who have the R&R trunk say that the liner really does have a second-skin like quality. That’s probably because the polyester blend fabric is stretchy, which felt more comfortable than Lululemon’s (also great!) Swim Short. These durable features also mean the R&R Trunk doubles as a decent gym short if you’re in a pinch, and saves you one less thing to pack for a tropical vacation. We love that it comes in 11 colorways, but if you want to go classic, you can’t go wrong with the Electric Blue or Navy option.

The absence of liner offers a comfortable commando style, which is why I prefer a pair like this one from Lululemon. I don’t have to be bothered with any mesh material that feels restrictive or scratchy against my crown jewels—I can just slip it on and head into the water. I also love that the minimal design doesn’t scream “swim trunk”, so I can go from brunch to the boardwalk or the pool without having to do an outfit change. It passes as an everyday short, which is exactly the kind of versatility I want in the summer. The polyester-elastomultiester fabric has so much stretch, it performs just as good—if not better—than most of my gym shorts.

I’ve worn this pair for pickup volleyball and quick workouts, and they move with you instead of clinging or sagging out. It also dries fast and doesn't get that heavy, waterlogged feel after a swim, which makes a huge difference if you’re posted up poolside for a while. The 7-inch inseam is short enough to show some quad, but long enough that it still feels put-together if you’re grabbing a drink after. On my 5’8” frame, it lands a couple inches above the knee with a clean, tailored look—not too baggy, not too slim. If you’re taller, it’ll read a bit shorter and sportier; shorter guys get that ideal mid-thigh cut without going full retro.
